The writer to the Hebrews does not stop at what is being removed; he tells you what you are receiving in its place. We are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken. While the made things fall away around us, an unshakable kingdom is being handed over into our hands.

Daniel had already seen it. In his vision a stone is cut out of a mountain without human hands, and it strikes the great statue of the empires and grinds it to chaff the wind carries off — and then the stone becomes a kingdom that shall never be destroyed and shall stand forever. That is the kingdom Hebrews says we are receiving. The shaking, then, is not pointless demolition after all. It is the clearing-away of everything breakable so that the one unbreakable kingdom can be seen for what it is, and taken hold of. And the right response, the writer says, is not panic. It is grateful, reverent worship.
voiceQuote: Receiving a kingdom that can't be shaken, let us have grace, whereby we may offer service well pleasing to God, with reverence and awe.
voiceAttribution: The letter to the Hebrews — Hebrews 12:28 (WEB)
scriptureText: In the days of those kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed... it shall stand forever.
weight:
Stand in the wreckage of your upheaval and do a hard, clarifying accounting. Everything the shaking has taken from you was, by definition, shakable — or it would still be standing. The certainties that cracked, the securities that gave way, the arrangements you leaned your weight on: they fell because they were made to fall. Grieve them honestly. But do not mistake them for the kingdom. They never were.

What you are left holding when the breakable things are gone is the only thing that was ever finally worth holding — a kingdom that cannot be moved. The temptation in any upheaval is to spend your strength clutching at what is already sliding away, as if gripping harder could make a shakable thing permanent. It cannot. So loosen your grip on the falling things, and receive the standing one. The proper posture in the rubble is not a white-knuckled fist; it is open hands, and reverence, and a strange and stubborn gratitude.

upheaval.thePhase: This is the telos over all four phases — what the whole shaking exists to leave standing, and a preview of where the series finally lands. Disconnect, disorientation, reorientation, reconnect: every phase is in service of this, the clearing of the breakable so the unbreakable kingdom can be received with thanks.
upheaval.inYou: Take the inventory honestly. Everything your upheaval stripped away was shakable, or it would not have gone. What remains in your open hands is the kingdom that cannot be moved, and it was always the only thing worth having. Receive it with awe instead of clutching after what was always going to fall.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church watching its structures tremble can forget that the kingdom is not the structures. The buildings, the programs, the familiar arrangements are all shakable; the kingdom they were built to serve is not. The rummage sale clears the breakable away so the body can take hold again of what stands forever.
upheaval.whatRemains: The kingdom that cannot be shaken — Daniel's stone that breaks the empires and stands forever, Christ and His unending reign. What cannot be shaken is, quite simply, this: the one kingdom you are receiving while everything else is being cleared away.
reflection: What has my upheaval taken that was, in the end, shakable?
Am I clutching at falling things, or receiving the kingdom that cannot be moved?
What would grateful, reverent worship look like from inside my rubble?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have been gripping the things that fall as though my grip could save them. Open my hands. Let me see that everything the shaking took was shakable, and that I am receiving a kingdom that cannot be moved. Teach me reverence and gratitude in the rubble. Amen.

notes.primary: Hebrews 12:28 (receiving a kingdom that can't be shaken); Daniel 2:44 (a kingdom that shall never be destroyed).

volumeSubtitle: Why God shakes what He loves
title: I make all things new
moment:
Listen closely to the words from the throne, because a single syllable carries the whole hope. The One seated there does not say, behold, I make all new things, as though the old order were so much rubbish to be hauled off and replaced with strangers. He says, behold, I make all things new. The same things. The very things. Made new. And then, as if to underline that this is not a poet's flourish, He gives an instruction: write it down, for these words are faithful and true. The promise is being certified, notarized, set in the record.

This is the trajectory of every upheaval God authors. Isaiah heard it too — new heavens and a new earth, so wholly renewed that the former griefs would not even come to mind. But notice that even there the canvas is heaven and earth, this heaven, this earth, not their replacement by some other thing. The shaking is severe, and it is real, and from inside it looks a great deal like destruction. But the destination is not the scrap heap. It is renewal. The wreckage is not discarded; it is the very material the renewing hand takes up and remakes.
voiceQuote: Behold, I make all things new... Write, for these words are faithful and true.
voiceAttribution: The One on the throne — Revelation 21:5 (WEB)
scriptureText: For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth; and the former things shall not be remembered, nor come into mind.
weight:
There is a lie that whispers in the worst of an upheaval, and it is this: you are being scrapped. Not refined, not rebuilt — scrapped, written off, headed for the heap so that something else can take your place. It is a plausible lie, because the early phases of any shaking really do feel like demolition with nothing on the other side. But it cannot survive the words from the throne. He does not make all new things. He makes all things new.

Which means the life the upheaval seems to be ruining is not being thrown away; it is being remade. The marriage, the faith, the calling, the self you fear is past saving — these are exactly the things the promise lays hold of. God is not in the business of discarding people and starting over with better stock. If He is in your shaking, its trajectory bends toward new, and the you that comes out the far side is not a stranger who replaced you. It is you, made new.

upheaval.thePhase: This is the telos and the hope that pulls every upheaval forward — the promise that draws the soul on through disorientation toward reorientation and reconnect. What it asks is faith in the direction of travel: to believe that the shaking, authored by God, is headed not toward the heap but toward all things made new.
upheaval.inYou: God is not scrapping you to start again with someone better. He makes all things new, and the all includes the very life the shaking seems to be wrecking. The trajectory of your upheaval, if He is in it, bends toward renewal, not toward the trash. You are being remade, not discarded.
upheaval.inTheBody: The church is not bound for the scrap pile, to be swapped out for some unrecognizable replacement. The same church, made new. Every rummage sale serves that promise — the old purified and remade, not thrown out for a stranger. What looks like the church's ending is the long work of its renewal.
upheaval.whatRemains: The One on the throne, and His certified word: I make all things new. What cannot be shaken is the trajectory itself — that in His hands the wreckage is raw material, and the end of every upheaval He authors is renewal, faithful and true.
reflection: Where have I believed the lie that my upheaval is scrapping me rather than remaking me?
What in my life feels past saving that the promise actually means to make new?
Can I trust that the same things, not different ones, are what God renews?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, in the worst of this I have believed I was being scrapped. But You do not make all new things; You make all things new. Take the very life I fear is ruined and remake it. Let me trust the direction of Your shaking, faithful and true. Amen.

notes.primary: Revelation 21:5 (behold, I make all things new); Isaiah 65:17 (new heavens and a new earth).

volumeSubtitle: Why God shakes what He loves
title: A new creation
era: What you become through the shaking
moment:
Paul hands the shaken Corinthians a sentence that turns demolition into birth: if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; the old things have passed away, and behold, they have become new. He does not say the old self is merely improved, or patched, or talked out of its worst habits. He says it passes away, and something genuinely new comes in its place. The verb is the same one God speaks from the throne — new — and Paul plants it in the present tense, in a living person, in the middle of a community still arguing and stumbling and being remade.

To the Galatians he draws the sharp edge of it. The old identity-markers that once decided everything — circumcision or uncircumcision, the badges by which they had always known who counted — are now worth precisely nothing. Neither this nor that, he says; only a new creation. So the shaking that dismantled the old self, that stripped away the markers and the certainties and the version of you that you had always answered to, was never simple destruction. It was the labor of a new creation being born. Upheaval, in Christ, is generative. The tearing-down is the contraction before the birth.
voiceQuote: If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, they have become new.
scriptureText: For neither is circumcision anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation.
weight:
When an upheaval comes for your sense of who you are — when the roles, the labels, the self-understanding you had built your life around all start coming apart — it feels like the unmaking of you. And in a sense it is. But here is the question that decides everything: which self is being unmade? Because the self the upheaval is dismantling is the old self, and Paul says the passing of the old self is not your death. It is your renewal.

This is the difference between an upheaval that ends in despair and one that ends in a new creation. Both feel like coming apart. But one reads the coming-apart as the end of the person, and one reads it as the old things passing away so the new can come. The second is the truth in Christ. The badges that are losing their grip on you were never the real you; they were the scaffolding. What feels like falling to pieces may be the only way the new creation gets free of the old one. You are not being destroyed. You are being born.

upheaval.thePhase: This belongs to reorientation flowing into reconnect — the new identity that emerges and settles on the far side of the shaking. What it asks is to let the old self go: to stop defending the markers and the former version of you, and to receive the new creation God is bringing up out of the wreckage of the old.
upheaval.inYou: The self the upheaval is taking apart is the old self, and its passing is not your destruction; it is your renewal. In Christ you are a new creation. What feels like falling to pieces may simply be the old things passing away so the new can come. Do not grieve the scaffolding as though it were the building.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church remade through upheaval is not just a battered version of the old one limping on. In Christ it is a new creation. The badges and boundaries that once told it who belonged count for far less now than the new thing God is making of it. The shaking has been creative all along, not only destructive.
upheaval.whatRemains: The new creation in Christ, and the Christ who creates it. What cannot be shaken is your standing in Him — the one identity an upheaval cannot dismantle, because He is not the old self the shaking takes, but the new self it is laboring to bring to birth.
reflection: Which self is my upheaval actually dismantling — and is it the old one I was meant to outgrow?
What identity-markers am I defending that count for nothing next to the new creation?
Can I read this coming-apart as a birth rather than a death?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, this shaking feels like the unmaking of me, and the old self clings hard. Remind me that in Christ I am a new creation, and that the old things passing away is renewal, not ruin. What is being torn apart is only the scaffolding. Bring the new creation to birth. Amen.

notes.primary: 2 Corinthians 5:17 (a new creation, the old passed away); Galatians 6:15 (not circumcision but a new creation).

volumeSubtitle: Why God shakes what He loves
title: The gate of heaven
moment:
Jacob is a man caught exactly between two lives. He has fled the home he cheated his way out of and has not yet reached the place he is running toward; he is nobody's, nowhere, asleep on the open ground with a stone for a pillow. It is the perfect picture of what later writers would name liminal space — the threshold between what was and what is not yet, the disorienting gap that Victor Turner and Richard Rohr both observed is where the deepest transformation tends to happen. Jacob would have rushed straight through it if he could.

And it is there, in the very gap he wants only to get past, that heaven opens. A ladder, angels ascending and descending, and the LORD Himself standing above it with a promise. Jacob wakes shaken, astonished that God had been in a place he had written off as empty transit: surely the LORD was in this place, and he did not know it. The nothing-place, the in-between he was sleeping through, turns out to be the house of God and the gate of heaven. He had been camping at the threshold of the holy and had nearly missed it.
voiceQuote: Surely the LORD is in this place, and I didn't know it.
scriptureText: How dreadful is this place! This is none other than God's house, and this is the gate of heaven.
weight:
Everything in you wants to rush the in-between. The gap between the old life and the new one — after the break, before the arrival — feels like wasted time, dead miles to be endured and forgotten, a waiting room with no magazines. So we sleep through it, or we numb it, or we throw all our energy at getting it over with, certain that nothing of value could possibly be happening in a place this formless and exposed.

But Bethel says otherwise. The threshold was exactly where Jacob met God — not back in the home he left, not ahead in the land he was promised, but there, in the disorienting middle he could not wait to escape. The in-between is not dead time to be survived; it can be the holiest ground you will ever stand on, the gate of heaven disguised as a nowhere with a stone for a pillow. So before you sleep through your wilderness or sprint to its exit, look around. The LORD may be in this very place you cannot wait to leave, and you do not yet know it.

upheaval.thePhase: This is disorientation — the liminal middle, the threshold between what was and what is not yet, and the holiness hidden inside it. What it asks is presence: not to numb or sprint through the in-between, but to stay awake in it, on the chance that the nowhere you are crossing is the gate of heaven.
upheaval.inYou: You want to rush the in-between, the disorienting stretch between the old life and the new. But the threshold is exactly where Jacob met God. Do not sleep through yours. The LORD may be in this very place you cannot wait to leave, and like Jacob you may simply not know it yet.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church in liminal space — no longer what it was, not yet what it will be — feels stranded, exposed, caught in the open with no clear address. But Bethel reframes the stranding. The threshold is holy ground, the gate of heaven. The in-between is not dead time for the body to grit through; it can be the place of encounter.
upheaval.whatRemains: The LORD standing over the ladder, present in the place that looked empty. What cannot be shaken is His presence in the gap itself — not only in the home behind or the land ahead, but here, in the disorienting middle, the gate of heaven you were about to sleep through.
reflection: Where am I rushing through an in-between, certain nothing of value could be happening there?
What might I be sleeping through that is actually the gate of heaven?
Can I stay awake to the holiness of the threshold I cannot wait to leave?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I want only to be through this in-between, to skip the disorienting middle and reach the other side. But You met Jacob at the threshold. Keep me awake in mine. Let me find that You are in this very place I cannot wait to leave, even when I do not yet know it. Amen.

notes.primary: Genesis 28:16-17 (surely the LORD is in this place; the gate of heaven).
notes.tradition: Touches the idea of liminal space (the threshold between what was and what will be), a theme developed by Victor Turner and Richard Rohr; paraphrased and attributed, with the anchor in Jacob's own words.

volumeSubtitle: Why God shakes what He loves
title: The day of small things
moment: Picture the scene at the second temple. The foundation is laid at last, after exile and ruin, and a shout goes up — but underneath the shout there is weeping. The old men who remember Solomon's house, the gold and the cedar and the glory of it, look at this modest rebuild and grieve at how small it has turned out to be. To them the new thing is an embarrassment beside the old. Into that mood the LORD speaks through Zechariah, and it lands like a gentle rebuke: who has despised the day of small things? The plummet, the little measuring weight, is in Zerubbabel's hand, and the eyes of the LORD are watching with delight over a beginning that everyone else finds disappointing. Jesus draws the same picture later with a seed. The Kingdom starts as the smallest of all the seeds, a thing you could lose in the crease of your palm, and yet it becomes the tree the birds of the air come and nest in. Renewal almost never arrives full-grown. It arrives small, easy to overlook, easy to scorn for not being what once was.
voiceQuote: Who has despised the day of small things? ... these are the eyes of the LORD, which run back and forth through the whole earth.
scriptureText: The Kingdom of Heaven is like a grain of mustard seed... which indeed is smaller than all seeds. But when it is grown, it is greater than the herbs, and becomes a tree.
weight: We have been trained to measure by the old grandeur, and so the first signs of God's new work look like failure. A handful where there were crowds. A flicker of hope where there was certainty. A foundation barely cleared where a cathedral once stood. And something in us wants to weep over the smallness rather than rejoice that anything is being built at all. But despising the day of small things is, finally, despising the way God almost always works. He is not impressed by scale the way we are. He delights in the seed, the plummet, the first faithful foundation laid by hands that could not finish the whole house in a day. So when the new thing in you or among you looks too small to matter, refuse the contempt. The eyes of the LORD are running over the earth, and they are not scanning for the impressive. They are resting, with joy, on the mustard seed nobody else noticed.

upheaval.thePhase: This is Reorientation — the phase where new bearings begin to form, but quietly, in beginnings so modest they are easy to write off. It asks you not to despise what God has only just started. The grandeur is not the test of His presence; the seed is enough, because of whose hand planted it.
upheaval.inYou: The first signs of the new thing in you will be unimpressive — a single restored habit, a thin thread of hope, a foundation barely laid. You will be tempted to despise them because they are not the old strength you remember. Do not. God loves to begin mustard-seed small, and what He begins He intends to grow into a tree.
upheaval.inTheBody: Renewal in a church usually starts tiny: a few gathered to pray, a small faithful remnant, a modest work nobody outside notices. Those who remember the fuller pews are tempted to grieve the smallness as decline. But the eyes of the LORD rejoice over the little beginning. The tree the next generation rests in is, right now, the smallest of seeds.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is not the scale of the work but the One whose eyes watch over it. Buildings and crowds rise and fall; the Kingdom that began as a seed will stand forever. When the small beginning is His, its smallness takes nothing from its future.
reflection: Where am I despising a small beginning because it is not the grandeur I remember?
What flicker of new life has God started in me that I have been too quick to dismiss?
Can I let the eyes of the LORD, and not the size of the work, decide what is worth rejoicing over?
upheaval.prayer: LORD, forgive me for despising the day of small things. Teach me to rejoice over the seed You have planted, even when it looks like nothing, and to trust that what You begin small You will grow in Your time. Amen.

notes.primary: Zechariah 4:10 (do not despise the day of small things); Matthew 13:31-32 (the mustard seed).

volumeSubtitle: Why God shakes what He loves
title: The remnant
moment: Isaiah is looking out over wreckage. The land is desolate, the cities are burned, the people are few — and he says a startling thing: if the LORD of Hosts had not left them a very small remnant, they would have become Sodom and Gomorrah, erased without a trace. The only reason Israel still exists at all is that God kept a few alive. Centuries later Paul reaches back for the very same word when he agonizes over whether God has abandoned his own people. No, he insists; even now, at this present time, there is a remnant according to the election of grace. The crowd has thinned, the visible numbers have collapsed, and yet the line of faith has not been broken, because it never did depend on the crowd. It is carried by the few God preserves. Through every upheaval the pattern repeats. Never the whole multitude, but never quite no one. A handful comes through the fire still holding the faith — not because they were stronger, but because grace kept them, a chosen seed planted on the far side of the shaking.
voiceQuote: Even so then, at this present time also, there is a remnant according to the election of grace.
scriptureText: Unless the LORD of Hosts had left to us a very small remnant, we would have been as Sodom; we would have been like Gomorrah.
weight: When an upheaval thins the ranks, the loss is loud, and it tells you a lie: that fewness is failure, that you are what was left over after the real thing collapsed. But the remnant has never been the leftover. It is the seed. It is the thread God draws deliberately through the eye of the disaster to stitch one era of faith to the next. You may be standing in a season where almost everyone you started with has fallen away or drifted off or stopped believing, and you feel less like a survivor than like debris. Hear it plainly: the remnant according to grace is not the church's embarrassment but its lifeline. The faith has crossed every chasm in its long history on the backs of a faithful few who looked, at the time, like nothing more than the last ones left. Being among the few is not a verdict against you. It may yet turn out to be the most important thing about you.

upheaval.thePhase: This bridges Disorientation and Reorientation. In the disorienting collapse, the remnant feels like nothing but loss; turning toward reorientation, it is revealed as God's chosen seed of the future. The phase asks you to stop reading fewness as failure and start trusting the One who keeps a remnant by grace, on purpose, every time.
upheaval.inYou: If your shaking has left you among the very few still holding on, do not read that as proof you have failed. The remnant has always been small, and always been God's instrument. You are not the leftover scraps of a faith that fell apart. By grace, you may be the seed God is carrying through to whatever comes next.
upheaval.inTheBody: The church has never once died out, because God always keeps a remnant through the shaking — a faithful few when the crowds melt away. A collapse in numbers is not the death of the church; it is the moment the remnant matters most. The faith has crossed every chasm on the shoulders of the few preserved by grace.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the faithfulness of God to keep a people for Himself. Crowds gather and scatter; the remnant He elects by grace endures. The line of faith does not survive on numbers but on the One who has never yet let it be wholly extinguished.
reflection: Have I been reading the smallness of the faithful around me as failure rather than as grace at work?
Where do I feel like leftover debris instead of a seed God is keeping on purpose?
Am I willing to be one of the few who carries the faith through, even if the crowd never returns?
upheaval.prayer: LORD of Hosts, when I feel like one of the last few left, remind me that You have always kept a remnant by grace. Hold me among them, and use even the few to carry Your faith through to the other side. Amen.

notes.primary: Romans 11:5 (a remnant according to grace); Isaiah 1:9 (a very small remnant left).

volumeSubtitle: Why God shakes what He loves
title: Test everything; hold fast the good
era: How to sift in the shaking
moment: Paul gives the Thessalonians an instruction with two halves, and most people only keep the first. Test all things — examine them, weigh them, refuse to swallow whole whatever you were handed. That half is easy to love in an upheaval; it gives permission to question everything, and questioning feels like freedom. But the sentence does not stop there. Hold firmly to that which is good. The testing has an aim, and the aim is not an empty pan. It is to keep the gold. John says the same to a church awash in voices: do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are of God, because plenty of false ones have gone out into the world. Notice that he commands discernment, not paralysis and not wholesale rejection. The work of coming through a shaking with your faith intact is sifting work — the patient labor of running the whole inheritance through your hands, letting the gravel fall, and closing your fist around what proves true. It is the opposite of both swallowing everything and smashing everything.
voiceQuote: Test all things, and hold firmly that which is good.
scriptureText: Don't believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are of God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world.
weight: There is a kind of upheaval that mistakes demolition for the goal — that treats the smashing as proof of honesty and counts an empty pan a kind of victory. But Paul will not let the sifting end there. Test all things, yes; and then hold fast to that which is good. If you are questioning everything you were ever taught, that is not faithlessness — it may be the most honest thing you have ever done. Only do not stop halfway and call the wreckage wisdom. The point of running the pan through the water is not to be left with nothing; it is to find the gold you can now trust precisely because you tested it and it held. Anyone can break a thing. Discernment is harder and slower: it keeps the treasure while it releases the dross, and it refuses to throw out what is true just because it came tangled up with what was false. Sift. Do not merely smash.

upheaval.thePhase: This sits between Disorientation and Reorientation — the discernment work of the in-between. It asks you to do the patient labor of sifting rather than the quick satisfaction of smashing. Reorientation is built not by destroying everything you inherited but by testing it all and keeping, with a firm grip, whatever proves to be good and true.
upheaval.inYou: If you are questioning everything you were given, good — test all things. But the command does not end at the questioning. Hold fast what is good. The goal of your sifting is not an empty hand and a cleared-out faith; it is the gold you can finally trust because you put it to the test and it stood. Keep what is true.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church re-examining its own tradition can sift or it can smash. Sifting tests everything and holds fast what is good, keeping the treasure while it lets the dross go. Smashing throws out the gold with the gravel and calls the rubble courage. The work the Spirit asks of a community in upheaval is discernment, not demolition.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the good itself — the true that survives every honest test. You are not the arbiter of what endures; you are the one who learns to recognize it. Test everything, and what is genuinely of God will still be standing in your hand when the sifting is done.
reflection: Am I testing what I was taught in order to keep the gold, or just to be rid of all of it?
What good have I been tempted to throw out simply because it came tangled with something false?
Where do I need to stop smashing and start the slower work of sifting?
upheaval.prayer: LORD, give me the patience to test all things and the courage to hold fast what is good. Keep me from mistaking demolition for discernment, and let me close my hand around the truth that survives the sifting, the gold I can now trust because You let it stand. Amen.

notes.primary: 1 Thessalonians 5:21 (test all things, hold fast the good); 1 John 4:1 (test the spirits).

volumeSubtitle: Why God shakes what He loves
title: It seemed good to the Spirit
moment: Around the year 49 the young church hits a question that could split it down the middle. Gentiles are streaming in, uncircumcised and untrained in the law, and a hard demand follows them: to belong, must they first become Jews? It is not a small dispute over procedure. It strikes at identity — who the people of God are and how anyone gets in. There is no clean precedent to settle it. And here is what the church does not do: it does not quietly fracture into two churches, and it does not bury the question under a forced peace. It gathers in Jerusalem and argues, openly and hard. Peter testifies, Paul and Barnabas tell what God has done, James weighs the Scriptures, and the assembly listens — for one another and, underneath that, for the Spirit. What emerges is a settlement they can put their name to together, in words that have echoed down the centuries ever since: it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us. Not a winner crushing a loser, and not a split into two. A body that discerned its way through.
voiceQuote: It seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us, to lay no greater burden on you than these necessary things.
scriptureText: My judgment is that we don't trouble those from among the Gentiles who turn to God.
weight: Most of us have only two moves when an upheaval raises a question our old framework cannot answer: bolt, or pretend. Bolt — walk out, split off, declare the others compromised. Or pretend — smother the question, keep the peace, act as though nothing is shaking. The Jerusalem council models a third way, and it is harder than both. Bring the question into the open. Let the disagreement be real and spoken, not whispered in corners. Listen, genuinely, to people who see it differently. And wait together for what seems good to the Spirit — not just to you, alone, certain, in a hurry, but to the Spirit and to the body discerning alongside you. It is slower than bolting and braver than pretending. Not every upheaval has to end in a rupture. Some of the most important ones in the history of God's people ended in a room where people argued honestly and then said, together, this seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us.

upheaval.thePhase: This belongs to Reorientation moving toward Reconnect — an upheaval that does not end in rupture but in a new, shared settlement. It asks for the patience of communal discernment: surfacing the hard question, hearing one another, and listening for the Spirit until a consensus the whole body can own emerges on the far side.
upheaval.inYou: When an upheaval forces a question your old framework cannot hold, the temptation is to bolt or to bury it. The Jerusalem way is neither. Bring it into the open, before God and a few you trust, and listen — patiently, without rushing to be right — for what seems good to the Spirit and to you together, not to you alone in a hurry.
upheaval.inTheBody: The first great rummage sale, the welcome of the Gentiles, shows a church navigating an identity-shaking change without shattering: honest disagreement, open debate, Spirit-led discernment, a settlement the whole body could name as its own. Not every upheaval has to end in a split. Acts 15 is the better pattern, and it is still available.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the Spirit who guides a listening body into truth. Opinions clash and consensus is hard-won, but the One who led the council still leads. When a community discerns together rather than fracturing, it leans on a guidance that does not fail.
reflection: When a hard question shakes me, do I bolt, pretend, or stay and discern?
Whom have I refused to truly listen to because I had already decided I was right?
Am I willing to wait for what seems good to the Spirit and to the body, not only to me alone?
upheaval.prayer: Holy Spirit, when upheaval raises questions I cannot answer alone, keep me from bolting and from pretending the question away. Teach me to listen, to discern in the company of others, and to wait for what seems good to You and to us together. Amen.

notes.primary: Acts 15:19, 28 (the Jerusalem Council; it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us).

volumeSubtitle: Why God shakes what He loves
title: Through the waters
figure: He who began a good work
moment: Here the frame closes. Over these first days you have been handed a map — the four phases, the two thresholds of soul and church, the promise that what can be shaken is shaken so that what cannot be shaken may remain. But a map is not the journey, and Isaiah is careful not to promise you will be spared the terrain. He does not say you will go around the waters or detour past the fire. He says when — when you pass through the waters, when you walk through the fire — and into that hard honesty he sets the only thing that finally matters: I will be with you. The rivers will not overflow you. The flame will not kindle on you. Not because the deep water and the fire are illusions, but because the LORD is in them with you. And beneath even that, Paul lays the floor of the whole undertaking. He is confident of one thing: the God who began a good work in you will be the very One to bring it to completion. You are not asked to finish yourself.
voiceQuote: When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow you; when you walk through the fire, you shall not be burned, neither shall the flame kindle on you.
scriptureText: being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.
weight: So you step off the edge of the frame and into the journey with two promises in your hands. The first is presence: whatever phase you are standing in — the break, the wilderness, the slow re-forming, the re-rooting — you will pass through, not around, and He will be with you in the passing. The waters are real and they will not drown you. The fire is real and it will not consume you. The second promise is the heavier one to believe and the more freeing: you do not have to complete the work. He who began it will finish it. That lifts the unbearable weight off your shoulders — the dread that if you falter, the whole thing collapses; that your upheaval is a test you might simply fail. It is not. The finishing belongs to God. Your part is to keep walking through, with the One who started the work and has promised to see it done.

upheaval.thePhase: This closes the frame and commissions you into all four phases at once. It does not name a single phase so much as hand you the map for every one of them. It asks only this: step into the journey trusting the God who is present in the waters and the fire, and who will complete the work He has begun in you.
upheaval.inYou: Whatever phase you are in — breaking, wandering, slowly re-forming, re-rooting — the promise holds. You pass through the waters and the fire, not around them, and He is with you in them, and they will not consume you. And the God who began the good work in you will be the One to complete it. The finishing is His task, not yours.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church stepping into its own upheaval walks under the same promise. It will pass through deep waters; it will not be overflowed. The God who began His good work in His people will bring it to completion. The map has been given; now the body walks it — through the waters, with the LORD beside it the whole way.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the faithfulness of God to finish what He starts. Maps can be lost and journeys can falter, but the One who began the good work will complete it. His presence in the fire and His commitment to the end are the floor beneath every phase of the shaking.
reflection: Which phase am I actually standing in right now — and am I trying to go around it instead of through?
Where have I been carrying the weight of finishing a work that belongs to God?
Can I trust that the One who began His work in me will be the One to complete it?
upheaval.prayer: LORD, You do not promise me a way around the deep water or the fire, but You promise to be with me in them. Walk with me through every phase, and finish the good work You began, for I cannot finish it myself. Amen.

notes.primary: Isaiah 43:2 (when you pass through the waters, I will be with you); Philippians 1:6 (he who began a good work will complete it).

title: The break
moment: Before the wilderness, before the new bearings, before any of the long work of being remade, there is a door, and it closes. That is where every upheaval starts. Watch the fishermen on the lakeshore in Luke's account: they have hauled the boats up onto the sand, and then, with no ceremony at all, they leave everything and follow. Not arrange everything, not wind everything down — leave it. The nets are still wet. The catch is still in the hull. And the men are already walking away. This is the first phase, and it has a name: Disconnect. It is the break, the rupture, the leaving. It is not yet the desert of not-knowing; that comes later. It is simply the moment the old life is set down on the shore and the back is turned. Paul gives the same motion a different verb: the call of God is a call to come out and be separate, to step clear of what has held you. The phrase assumes there is somewhere you are still standing that you are meant to walk away from. The first move of God on a soul, and on a church, is almost always that: a leaving before it is ever an arriving.
voiceQuote: When they had brought their boats to land, they left everything, and followed him.
voiceAttribution: Luke, of the first disciples — Luke 5:11 (WEB)
scriptureText: Come out from among them, and be separate, says the Lord; touch no unclean thing, and I will receive you.
weight: It helps, more than you would think, to know which phase you are in. When your life breaks open, the temptation is to read the whole of it off the first chapter — to take the leaving for the entire story and conclude that loss is all there is. It is not. You have left; you have not yet arrived; and the ache between those two facts is not a sign that something has gone wrong. It is exactly what this first phase feels like from the inside. Name it, and it stops being a formless dread and becomes a recognizable place on the map. The door that closed behind you was not the end of the road. It was the beginning of one. So if you are standing on the far side of some rupture with the old life still in view across the water and nothing visible ahead — if you have come out but not yet come into — you are not lost. You are in Disconnect, the break that opens the work. The leaving is real. It is also only the first thing.

upheaval.thePhase: This is Disconnect, the first of the four phases: the break, the rupture, the leaving of the old behind. It does not ask you to understand where you are going. It asks only that you let the door close, set the nets on the shore, and come out — trusting that a leaving authored by God is the opening of a work, not the end of one.
upheaval.inYou: Your upheaval began with a break — something left, ruptured, walked away from, or torn out of your hands. Name it for what it is: the first phase, not the whole of the story. You have come out; you have not yet come in. That hollow ache between the two is not failure. It is simply what Disconnect feels like while you are standing in it.
upheaval.inTheBody: Every reformation opens the same way — a coming out, a separating, a leaving of the old arrangement before any new vitality arrives. The church's rummage sales begin in rupture long before they become renewal. When a community feels the old settlement crack and break, that is not the failure of the work. It is the start of it, the door closing so another can open.
upheaval.whatRemains: When the old life is set on the shore and the new one is nowhere in sight, what cannot be shaken is the One who issued the call. The leaving is His doing, not your undoing. He does not summon a soul out of one place without intending, in His own time, to bring it into another.
reflection: What did my upheaval ask me to leave on the shore, and have I actually let it go?
Am I reading the whole of my story off this first chapter of leaving?
Can I trust that coming out is the start of God's work in me, not the proof of His absence?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, You have called me out, the door has closed behind me, and I cannot yet see the road ahead. Help me set the old life down on the shore and follow, trusting that a leaving You author is the opening of Your work. Hold me in the break until You bring me through. Amen.

notes.primary: Luke 5:11 (they left everything and followed); 2 Corinthians 6:17 (come out and be separate).

title: Burn the plow
moment: The plow is the thing to watch. Elijah finds Elisha out in the field behind twelve yoke of oxen, throws the prophet's mantle across his shoulders, and keeps walking. And Elisha, called, does something more violent than simply leaving the farm. He takes the oxen he has been driving and slaughters them. He breaks up the wooden plowing gear and builds a fire with it. He boils the meat over the burning equipment, feeds it to the people, and then goes after Elijah. Look at what he has done. He has not asked for a leave of absence. He has destroyed the tools of his trade and eaten the means of his own retreat. There is no farm to slink back to now, no oxen, no plow, no quiet fallback if the prophetic life proves hard. He has burned the road behind him. Centuries later Jesus puts the same truth in a single line: the one who sets a hand to the plow and keeps glancing back over his shoulder has no place in the Kingdom of God. A break that leaves the plow standing in the field, ready for the day you change your mind, is not yet a break. It is a pause with an exit.
voiceQuote: He took the yoke of oxen, and killed them, and boiled their flesh with the instruments of the oxen, and gave to the people... then he arose, and went after Elijah.
scriptureText: No one, having put his hand to the plow, and looking back, is fit for the Kingdom of God.
weight: There is a kind of leaving that keeps a road open behind it, and that open road will pull at you with a strength you do not expect. The job you half-quit. The relationship you ended but did not close. The old certainty you set aside but kept within reach, just in case. As long as the plow still stands in the field, some part of you is farming with one eye on it — and the old life, given any opening at all, will quietly come back and reclaim you while you assure yourself you have moved on. This is the hard mercy of the decisive break. Some disconnects have to be made total, the oxen slaughtered and the plow burned, precisely because a half-leaving is no leaving at all. It is not that God delights in burning your bridges. It is that He knows the road back, left intact, is the road you will take the first time the new way frightens you. The break that holds is the one that closes the door so firmly there is nothing left to drift toward.

upheaval.thePhase: This is Disconnect at its most decisive: the break that destroys the road back. The phase does not always ask for a half-step that keeps the old life in reserve. Sometimes it asks for the plow on the fire — the deliberate closing of the way of retreat, so that you cannot quietly undo the leaving the moment it costs you something.
upheaval.inYou: A half-left thing keeps a road open behind you, and that road will pull harder than you think. Be honest about which of your breaks are real and which are only paused. Some have to be made total — the plow burned, the exit shut — or the old life will reach back and reclaim you while you tell yourself, comfortably, that you have already moved on.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church that half-reforms, keeping one discreet road back to the old comfort, rarely changes for long; the moment renewal grows costly, the congregation drifts back down the road it never closed. The breaks that hold in a community are the decisive ones — where the bridge is genuinely burned and there is simply nothing left to retreat toward.
upheaval.whatRemains: When the plow is burning and the road back is gone, what cannot be shaken is the One who threw the mantle across your shoulders. He does not call a soul out and then abandon it on a road with no return. The way back is closed; the One ahead is sure. He is reason enough to burn the plow.
reflection: Which of my breaks are genuinely decisive, and which still leave the plow standing in the field?
What road have I kept open behind me, just in case the new way proves hard?
Is the old life quietly reclaiming me while I tell myself I have already left it?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have made breaks that left a road open behind me, and I feel that road pulling even now. Give me courage to burn the plow — to close the way back, to slaughter the comfort I keep in reserve — and to follow without one eye on the field I left. Amen.

notes.primary: 1 Kings 19:21 (Elisha slaughters his oxen and burns the plow to follow Elijah); Luke 9:62 (no one looking back is fit for the Kingdom).

title: Abram goes
moment: He is seventy-five years old, and the LORD tells him to go. Picture Abram in Haran: settled, prosperous, deep into a life with a name and a place and people who know him. He has every earthly reason to stay and not one obvious reason to leave. And the word that comes is almost cruel in what it withholds — get out of your land, away from your kindred, out of your father's house, toward a land that I will show you. Show you. Later. The destination is named only as a promise and a direction; it has no place on any road Abram knows. He is told what to leave with perfect clarity and where to go with none at all. And he goes. Stephen, recounting it generations later, keeps the bare astonishment of it intact: God said get out, come into a land I will show you, and the man went. This is the archetype of the whole first phase, the pattern under all the others. The first move of faith is a leaving, made toward a place God has deliberately chosen not to disclose. Abram does not get the map. He gets the call, and the One who issues it, and that is made to be enough.
voiceQuote: So Abram went, as the LORD had spoken to him; and Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed out of Haran.
scriptureText: Get out of your land, and from your relatives, and come into a land which I will show you.
weight: God very often calls you out before He shows you where to. This is not an oversight in the arrangement; it is the arrangement. The disconnect comes first, clear and costly, while the destination stays folded in His hand, withheld on purpose. And everything in you wants to reverse the order — to be shown the land, surveyed and certain, before you will consent to leave Haran. But that is not how faith moves, and it never has been. Faith is not standing at the edge of the known, waiting for the fog over the future to clear before you take a step. Faith is going anyway, while it is still foggy, on the strength of the One who called. The withheld map is not God being secretive or unkind. It is God training a settled soul to walk by trust in a Person rather than by sight of a plan. If you wait to leave until you can see where you are going, you will never leave at all. Abram was seventy-five, comfortable, and right to stay by every visible measure. He went. So can you.

upheaval.thePhase: This is Disconnect as archetype: leaving the known for a land not yet named. The phase will not hand you the destination before it asks for the departure. It asks you to do what Abram did — to obey the call to go while the where is still withheld, walking out of your settled Haran on the strength of the One who promises to show you, in time.
upheaval.inYou: God often calls you out before He shows you where to. The disconnect comes first; the destination stays folded in His hand. Faith is not waiting at the door until the road ahead clears — it is going anyway, while the fog still hangs, as Abram went, on the strength of the One who called and not on the strength of a map you do not yet hold.
upheaval.inTheBody: The people of God have always been a pilgrim people, summoned out before the destination came clear. A church clutching its Haran — its settled, prosperous, comfortable familiarity — cannot follow a God whose first word is so often the bare command to go. Renewal asks a community to leave the known before the new land is named, or it does not leave at all.
upheaval.whatRemains: When the map is withheld and only the call remains, what cannot be shaken is the One doing the calling. Abram had no coordinates; he had the LORD, and that proved the surer thing. The destination can stay hidden and the road foggy, and still the ground holds, because the One who said go goes with you.
reflection: Where is God calling me out before He has shown me where to, and am I refusing to move until I see the map?
What is my Haran — the settled, prosperous familiarity I am clutching against the call to go?
Can I trust the One who calls enough to leave before the destination is named?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, You have called me out and withheld the map, and I want to see the land before I leave my Haran. Teach me to walk as Abram walked — by trust in You, not by sight of a plan. Let Your call alone be enough to make me go. Amen.

notes.primary: Genesis 12:4 (Abram went, at seventy-five, out of Haran); Acts 7:3 (Stephen recounts the call: get out of your land).

title: Forget your father's house
moment: The hardest part of a disconnect is almost never the geography. It is the people. You can leave a city, a job, a whole way of life, and the sharpest pain in the leaving will still be the faces. The psalmist knows it. In the wedding song of Psalm 45 the bride is given a strange and tender charge on the threshold of her new life: she is to set aside even her own kin, the father's house that raised her. Not because that house was wicked, but because the new covenant cannot be fully entered while she keeps one foot in the old belonging. Jesus says something harder still, and means the same thing: anyone who loves father or mother, son or daughter, more than Him is not worthy of Him. It lands like cruelty until you see what it is doing. He is not saying kin counts for nothing. He is saying that a break which costs you nothing at the level of belonging is usually not a real break at all. The severance that actually hurts, the one reaching into the circle that shaped and loved you, is the one the first phase most often requires. The sharpest cut of any leaving is the human one.
voiceQuote: Listen, daughter, consider, and turn your ear; forget your own people, and also your father's house.
voiceAttribution: The psalmist, to the bride — Psalm 45:10 (WEB)
scriptureText: He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and he who loves son or daughter more than me isn't worthy of me.
weight: Your upheaval may well cost you belonging, and you should not be surprised when it does. The approval of the very people who formed you. The warmth of a circle you have stood inside your whole life. The unspoken sense of being one of us, held by a tribe that no longer fits the place God is taking you. When the break severs that, the grief is not a sign you have chosen wrongly; it is the measure of how real the leaving is. Do not let anyone, least of all yourself, shame you for the pain of it — the loss of belonging is among the deepest a person can carry. And yet. Sometimes that very severance is the most necessary part of the break, and the most faithful. A loyalty to kin that quietly overrules the call of God has stopped being love and become an anchor. Honor what it costs you. Grieve the faces. But do not let even the dearest belonging hold you in a Haran that God has plainly told you to leave. The deepest cut can also be the truest obedience.

upheaval.thePhase: This is Disconnect counting its sharpest cost: the price the break exacts on belonging and family. The phase does not ask you to despise the people who shaped you. It asks you to love God more than even them — to accept that a leaving which severs nothing relationally is rarely a real leaving, and that the human cut is often the necessary one.
upheaval.inYou: Your upheaval may cost you belonging — the approval of the very people who shaped you, the warmth of a circle that no longer fits where God is taking you. That severance is the deepest pain of the break, and the grief of it is honest. Do not despise the cost. But do not let the dearest belonging keep you where God has told you to leave, either.
upheaval.inTheBody: Leaving an old religious belonging — a tradition, a tribe, the community that first raised you in the faith — can feel exactly like betraying family, and the grief that comes with it is real and worth honoring. Do not pretend it away. But sometimes the break from the father's house is precisely the call, and a community clutching its kin can refuse the very God it claims to follow.
upheaval.whatRemains: When belonging is the price and the dearest faces fall away, what cannot be shaken is the One who said to love Him first. He does not strip a soul of every circle to leave it alone; He becomes, Himself, the belonging beneath all belonging. The father's house may be left behind. The Father is not.
reflection: What belonging is my upheaval costing me, and am I grieving it honestly rather than pretending it does not hurt?
Where has loyalty to the people who shaped me quietly begun to overrule the call of God?
Can I love the faces I am leaving and still love God more?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, the hardest part of this break is the people — the faces, the belonging, the circle that shaped me. I grieve the cost and will not pretend it does not hurt. Yet teach me to love You more than even them, and be Yourself the belonging beneath all I am losing. Amen.

notes.primary: Psalm 45:10 (forget your people and your father's house); Matthew 10:37 (love for Christ above kin).

title: Go forward
moment: Stand at the edge of the sea with the whole nation, and feel the trap. Behind them, the dust of Pharaoh's chariots is rising on the horizon; the empire that held them four hundred years is bearing down to drag them back. Ahead lies water, wide and impassable. They are pried loose at last from the only home they have ever known — and that home was a house of slavery, a comfortable misery they had half-learned to call life. Now they are out, and terrified, and Moses is crying out to God. And the LORD's word to him is not what anyone at that shoreline expects. It is not pray harder. It is not stand and wait for rescue. It is this: why cry to me? Tell the children of Israel to go forward. Move. Into the dead end. And here is the mercy folded inside the command — they are not sent out blind or alone. From the night they left, the LORD has gone ahead of them, cloud by day and fire through the dark, leading the way. This is Scripture's great communal disconnect, an entire people wrenched out of bondage in a single night. And the wrenching is not random, not abandoned. It is led.
voiceQuote: The LORD said to Moses, Why do you cry to me? Speak to the children of Israel, that they go forward.
scriptureText: The LORD went before them by day in a pillar of cloud, to lead them on their way, and by night in a pillar of fire.
weight: Sometimes the only road out of a bondage runs straight forward, into what looks for all the world like a dead end. You keep waiting for the way to open before you move; the LORD keeps saying move, and the way opens as you go. This is its own hard grace. The command in the break is rarely stand still until it is safe. It is go forward — step toward the very thing you most fear, the water, the unknown, the place with no visible road through it. And what makes that obedience possible is not your courage but the pillar. You are not the first one into the dead end. The One who called you out of your Egypt has already gone ahead into the exact place you are most afraid to step, cloud by day and fire by night, leading from the front, not driving from behind. So when the empire is at your back and the sea is in your face and every instinct screams retreat, hear the word again: go forward. The way out is forward, and the One you are following is already there.

upheaval.thePhase: This is Disconnect on the largest scale: the great corporate break, a whole people wrenched out of bondage at once. The phase does not always ask the soul to wait — at the edge of the sea it commands the people to move. It asks for forward motion into the dead end, trusting that the God who authored the departure has already gone ahead to lead it.
upheaval.inYou: Sometimes the only way out of a bondage is forward — straight into what looks like a dead end, with the old empire closing in behind you. The command in the break is not to freeze but to move, trusting the One who has already gone ahead of you, cloud and fire, into the very place you are most afraid to step. Go forward. He is there.
upheaval.inTheBody: A whole people can be enslaved to the familiar — even to a comfortable misery they have learned to call home. God's renewal of a community is often an exodus: a wrenching, divinely led departure out of a bondage they had made peace with, toward a promise they cannot yet see. The corporate break is frightening, and it is real, and it is led from the front.
upheaval.whatRemains: When the empire is behind and the sea ahead, what cannot be shaken is the pillar going on before — the LORD Himself, leading the break He authored. The corporate disconnect is neither random nor abandoned. The One who said go forward has already gone first into the dead end, and the cloud and the fire do not fail.
reflection: Where is God commanding me to go forward into what looks like a dead end, while I keep waiting for the way to open first?
What comfortable misery have I half-learned to call home rather than leave?
Can I trust that the One who called me out has already gone ahead of me into the place I most fear?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, the old empire is at my back and the sea is in my face, and everything in me wants to retreat to the bondage I knew. Give me faith to go forward at Your word, trusting that You have already gone ahead — cloud by day, fire by night. Lead me through. Amen.

notes.primary: Exodus 14:15 (tell the people to go forward); Exodus 13:21 (the pillar of cloud and fire leading them out).

title: Eaten in haste
moment:
Picture the meal. It is the strangest supper in Scripture, because no one sits down. The lamb is roasted, the bread is flat because there was no time to let it rise, and the LORD's instruction is precise about how to eat it: belt fastened, sandals already on the feet, walking-staff in hand, the whole thing swallowed standing and fast. This is not a feast to linger over. It is rations bolted by people who expect, at any moment, to hear the door thrown open and a voice say go.

And that is exactly what happens. At midnight the blow falls on Egypt, and before dawn Pharaoh is summoning Moses in the dark, telling Israel to rise up and get out and serve their God. The window opens suddenly and it does not stay open long. Four hundred years of slavery end in a single night, and the people who walk free are the ones who ate dressed for the road. The ones who had settled in for a long night, who had unlaced their sandals and banked the fire, would have missed it. Deliverance came at the speed of a door swinging open.
voiceQuote: With your loins girded, your shoes on your feet, and your staff in your hand, you shall eat it in haste; it is the LORD's Passover.
voiceAttribution: The LORD, instituting the Passover — Exodus 12:11 (WEB)
scriptureText: Rise up, get out from among my people... and go, serve the LORD, as you have said.
weight:
Some deliverances have a narrow window, and they do not announce themselves in advance. You cannot schedule the night the door opens; you can only be dressed for it or not. The hard truth underneath the Passover is that readiness is a posture you hold before you have any proof you will need it — sandals on through a long, ordinary evening, on the strength of a promise that tonight might be the night.

Most of us would rather get comfortable. We unpack in the very Egypt God is calling us out of; we tell ourselves the move is coming and meanwhile we settle deeper into what we mean to leave. But the break, when it comes, tends to come fast, and comfort is slow to its feet. The question Disconnect puts to you is not whether you believe deliverance is coming. It is whether you would be standing, staff in hand, if it came tonight — or still asleep with your shoes off.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect asks for readiness. Before the wilderness, before the new land, there is a door that will open suddenly, and the phase requires you to stand dressed for the road. The break rewards the poised and passes by the settled. Faithfulness here looks like sandals on, waiting, when the night is still ordinary.
upheaval.inYou: The window of your deliverance may be narrow. Do not unpack in the Egypt God is leading you out of, sinking into the very comfort you mean to leave. Hold the posture of departure — alert, lightly held, dressed for the road — so that when the door swings open you are on your feet and moving, not fumbling for your shoes.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church waiting on renewal must be dressed for the road too — not so wedded to its building, its budget, its inherited habits that it cannot move the night God opens the door. Readiness to leave the old behind is not faithlessness; it is faithfulness. A people too settled to travel will sleep straight through their own deliverance.
upheaval.whatRemains: Beneath the haste and the narrow window stands the LORD who opens the door at all. The night belongs to Him; the timing is His. What cannot be shaken is not your alertness but His deliverance — sure to come, sudden when it comes, and worth standing dressed for through every long and ordinary evening.
reflection: Am I dressed for the road, or have I unpacked and settled into the very Egypt God is calling me out of?
What comfort am I sinking into that would slow me down if the door opened tonight?
Do I believe my deliverance is coming enough to stand ready before I can see it?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have grown comfortable in the place You mean to lead me out of, my shoes off, the fire banked. Find me standing instead, dressed for the road, staff in hand. When You open the door, let me be on my feet and ready to go at the speed of Your deliverance. Amen.

notes.primary: Exodus 12:11 (eat the Passover in haste, dressed to travel); Exodus 12:31 (Pharaoh: rise up and go).

title: Into the sea
moment:
They are trapped, and they know it. Behind them the dust of Pharaoh's chariots is rising; ahead of them the sea spreads out wide and deep and impassable. This is the full terror of the break laid bare: no road back, and the only road forward runs straight into water that will drown them. Israel does the human thing and panics, and Moses says the words that have steadied the cornered ever since — do not be afraid, stand still, and watch what the LORD will do.

Then the wind comes, and the waters open, and a corridor of dry ground appears with walls of sea standing on either hand. But here is the part we hurry past: the miracle does not carry them across. It only makes a way. They still have to walk into it — down between two towering walls of water that hang there by nothing they can see, that could close at any second and bury them in the deep. Every step is taken on ground that was seabed an hour ago, under a weight of water held back by a power they cannot verify. The salvation is real. It also looks, from inside the corridor, exactly like walking into your own drowning.
voiceQuote: Don't be afraid. Stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD, which he will work for you today.
scriptureText: The children of Israel went into the midst of the sea on the dry ground, and the waters were a wall to them on their right hand, and on their left.
weight:
The break can strand you in precisely this place — where retreat has become impossible and advance is terrifying, where the old life is pursuing from behind and the way out leads through deep water. You keep waiting for a path that does not frighten you. Often the only path on offer is the parted sea: real, and solid underfoot, and lined with walls that every instinct insists will fall.

Faith here is not the absence of fear; it is walking in afraid. It is putting weight on ground you were told is dry while your eyes report a wall of water that should not be standing. The decisive step of a disconnect rarely feels like rescue while you are taking it. It feels like stepping off the edge of the world. But the dry ground holds. And what was chasing you — the thing you were sure would catch you — does not make it onto the far shore.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect brings you to the threshold where back is impossible and through is the only way out. The phase asks for the terrifying step: into the parted water, between the standing walls, on a path that looks like death. It does not promise the fear will lift before you move. It promises the ground will hold.
upheaval.inYou: Your break may leave you cornered, the old life closing in behind and deep water ahead. Do not wait for a way that does not scare you; it may not come. Walk into the parted sea anyway, trusting the ground is real and solid beneath you, even as every nerve insists you are stepping straight into your own drowning.
upheaval.inTheBody: A community at the edge of real change knows this terror intimately — the familiar past pursuing hard behind, the unknown gaping ahead. The crossing frightens everyone in it, and no honest leader pretends otherwise. But the dry ground holds a whole people, and the thing that chased them out did not follow them onto the far shore.
upheaval.whatRemains: Beneath the walls of water that might fall stands the One who parted them and holds them. What cannot be shaken is not the corridor, which is temporary, but the salvation working through it. The ground holds because He holds it, and the deep that terrifies you obeys the hand that made you a way.
reflection: Where has my break stranded me, with no road back and only deep water ahead?
Am I waiting for a way that will not frighten me, when the parted sea is the only path on offer?
Can I walk in afraid, trusting the ground will hold even as it looks like drowning?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I am cornered, the old life behind me and deep water ahead, and the way You have opened looks like the place I will drown. Steady me to walk into it. Hold back what would bury me, make the ground solid under my feet, and let me reach the far shore. Amen.

notes.primary: Exodus 14:13 (stand still and see the salvation of the LORD); Exodus 14:22 (Israel walks into the sea on dry ground).

title: Your people, my people
moment:
Two widows stand on a road out of Moab, and a third has already turned back. Naomi has nothing left to offer — no husband, no sons, no future a young woman could build on — and she says so plainly, urging her daughters-in-law to return to their mothers, their gods, their own people, where a Moabite woman might yet be cared for. Orpah weeps and goes, and no one blames her; she is doing the sensible thing. But Ruth will not be sent home. She clings to Naomi and answers in words that have outlived every kingdom of that age: where you go, I will go; your people will be my people, and your God my God.

This is a break, but notice what kind. Ruth is not fleeing something terrible. Moab is her home, her gods are her gods, her whole conceivable future lies behind her on that road. She leaves all of it — homeland, religion, the prospect of remarriage and security — not to escape, but to cleave: to a destitute old woman with nothing to give her, and to an unfamiliar God chosen on the strength of love alone. She binds the choice with an oath that only death may break. It is one of Scripture's most beautiful disconnects.
voiceQuote: Don't entreat me to leave you... for where you go, I will go; and where you lodge, I will lodge; your people shall be my people, and your God my God.
scriptureText: Where you die, will I die, and there will I be buried; the LORD do so to me, and more also, if anything but death part you and me.
weight:
We tend to assume a break must be a flight — from something wrong, something harmful, something we are right to leave. But not every disconnect is an escape. Some are the opposite: a cleaving to something good that simply happens to cost you everything familiar. Ruth's leaving is not driven by what she is running from. It is drawn by whom she has decided to belong to, and the price is her entire former world.

This is the gentlest and sometimes the hardest break of all, because nothing forces it. No tyrant drives you out, no famine, no crisis. There is only love, asking whether you will bind yourself to it at the cost of the life you knew. That kind of leaving can feel reckless to everyone watching, the way Orpah's return felt wise. But the costly yes of love is not recklessness. Sometimes it is the most faithful step you will ever take, and the one God has waited longest to see you take.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect is not always a flight from harm; sometimes it is a cleaving chosen for love. The phase here asks the costliest yes — to leave the familiar not because it is wrong but because covenant love calls you elsewhere. The break of joining can cost as much as any escape, and it is freely given.
upheaval.inYou: Not every leaving in your life is a running-from. Some breaks are a cleaving-to — binding yourself, at the cost of everything familiar, to something or someone good. Do not mistake that price for a mistake. Love sometimes requires the break, and the costly yes you are most afraid of may be the most faithful step you ever take.
upheaval.inTheBody: The people of God has always grown by such cleavings — outsiders who leave their old belonging to join, at real cost to themselves and no compulsion but love. Ruth the Moabite becomes great-grandmother to David, and her costly yes runs straight into the line of the Messiah. The break of joining is how the family of faith keeps widening.
upheaval.whatRemains: Beneath a break made for love stands the God worth leaving everything to reach. What cannot be shaken is the covenant Ruth swore herself into — the binding that outlasts the homeland she left and the future she surrendered. The familiar world can fall away entirely, and the One you cleave to remains.
reflection: Is a break in my life a flight from something wrong, or a cleaving to something good that simply costs me everything familiar?
What costly yes have I been calling reckless when it may be the most faithful step I could take?
Whom, or what, is love asking me to bind myself to at the price of the world I knew?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have feared the break that costs me everything familiar, even when it is love and not harm that calls me out. Give me Ruth's courage to cleave — to say where You go I will go, and let the old world fall away. Bind me to You by a covenant that only death may break. Amen.

notes.primary: Ruth 1:16-17 (where you go I will go; your people shall be my people).

title: How long will you limp?
moment:
The whole nation is summoned to Mount Carmel, and Elijah opens with a question that lands like a blow. How long will you go limping between two opinions? It is the perfect picture of where Israel has lived for years: not openly rejecting the LORD, not openly serving Baal, but hobbling along with a foot in each, calling the lameness balance. Elijah will not let it stand. If the LORD is God, follow Him; if Baal, follow him — but choose. The crowd says nothing. There is nothing to say; he has named exactly what they have been avoiding.

So he forces the matter into the open. Two altars, two bulls, and the simple test: the God who answers by fire is God. Baal's prophets call all morning and cut themselves and get silence. Then Elijah soaks his altar until it streams with water, prays once, and the fire of the LORD falls and consumes everything — the offering, the wood, the stones, the very dust, and the water in the trench. And at last the divided heart breaks. The people fall on their faces and the cry goes up, the one thing they had refused to settle for years: the LORD, He is God; the LORD, He is God.
voiceQuote: How long will you waver between the two sides? If the LORD is God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him.
scriptureText: When all the people saw it, they fell on their faces; and they said, the LORD, he is God; the LORD, he is God.
weight:
An upheaval has a way of forcing the exact decision you have spent years avoiding — the divided loyalty you have nursed because choosing felt too costly, the half-and-half arrangement you have been calling wisdom. You tell yourself you can keep both. The LORD and the idol. The faith and the escape hatch. The conviction and the quiet compromise that contradicts it. Carmel says you cannot, not forever. At some point the limping has to end.

This is why the break, for a divided heart, is mercy disguised as demand. It does not multiply your options; it strips them down to one. It will not let you keep hobbling between two gods and calling it peace. The fire that falls is frightening, but what it ends is worse — the slow, exhausting half-life of a heart that will not choose. The disconnect here is simply this: choosing, at last, and letting the other thing go down with the false altar.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect forces the decision a divided heart keeps dodging. The phase ends the limping between two opinions and demands the break with the idol you have kept on the side. It will not let you call your lameness balance any longer. What it asks is plain and costly: choose, and let the other altar fall.
upheaval.inYou: Your upheaval may force the very choice you have avoided for years — the divided loyalty you have nursed because deciding felt too expensive. You cannot finally serve both; the limping cannot go on. The break is choosing at last, naming which God you will follow, and letting the other thing go down rather than keeping it quietly alive on the side.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church syncretized with the idols of its age — power, comfort, nation, brand — is limping between two opinions and calling it balance. Renewal demands the Carmel break: a decisive, public return to the LORD alone, with the rival altars actually torn down. A people that will not choose its God has, in the avoiding, already half-chosen the idol.
upheaval.whatRemains: Beneath the forced and frightening choice stands the God who answers by fire and proves Himself the only One worth choosing. What cannot be shaken is His sole and living Godhead — the LORD, He is God. The idol that limped beside Him all along was never real, and the fire that ends the divided heart reveals it.
reflection: What divided loyalty have I nursed for years because choosing felt too costly?
Where am I calling my lameness balance, hobbling between two gods and refusing to settle which is mine?
What rival altar do I need to let fall so I can follow the LORD alone?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have limped between two opinions and called it balance, keeping an idol quietly alive beside You because choosing felt too costly. End the lameness. Send the fire that forces my hand, and let the other altar fall. I choose You; You are God, and there is no other. Amen.

notes.primary: 1 Kings 18:21 (how long will you waver between two opinions?); 1 Kings 18:39 (the LORD, he is God).

title: Let justice roll down
moment:
Amos has no credentials for what God hands him. He is a herdsman from Tekoa and a tender of sycamore figs, a working man from the rural south, when the LORD takes him from following the flock and sends him north to Israel — prosperous, well-fed, religious Israel, at the height of its comfort. He arrives as an outsider to puncture a fat self-satisfaction, and his message is not gentle. Through him God says something almost unthinkable about the nation's worship: I hate, I despise your feasts; take away the noise of your songs. The crowded festivals, the polished liturgy, the busy religious calendar — God says He cannot stand them.

What does He want instead? Not more religion. Justice, rolling down like waters, and righteousness like a stream that never runs dry. The break Amos carries is itself a break from worship-as-usual: a rupture aimed not at irreligion but at religion grown comfortable and unjust, singing on Sunday and grinding the poor on Monday. His own life is the first thing ruptured — pulled from the flock, sent where he never trained to go — and the word he brings ruptures everyone who hears it. Some disconnects God authors are precisely a break from religion as we have always done it.
voiceQuote: Let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like a mighty stream.
scriptureText: I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was a herdsman; and the LORD took me from following the flock, and said to me, Go, prophesy to my people Israel.
weight:
Holy discontent has a way of rupturing the comfortable arrangement and sending you somewhere you never trained to go. It does not check your résumé first, and it does not wait until you feel qualified. The break can fall on the most ordinary person — mid-life, mid-career, no title, no platform, no theological pedigree — and put a word in your mouth that, once spoken, cannot be unheard, by you or by anyone who hears it.

And it can fall on the most religious of settings precisely because they are comfortable. We assume God's rupture targets the godless and leaves the devout in peace. Amos says otherwise.
