The shaking here is aimed straight at the fat, prosperous, busily worshiping community that has divorced its songs from its justice — that loves the festival and forgets the poor. So if your settled religious life is being disturbed, do not assume the disturbance is the enemy. It may be the herdsman's word arriving at your own door: take away the noise, and let justice roll.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect can be holy discontent rupturing a complacent, comfortable religion. The phase here breaks not the irreligious but the settled and self-satisfied — worship grown fat and unjust. It asks you to let the disturbance do its work: to hear, in the disruption of religion-as-usual, the very voice of God calling the comfortable off their festivals.
upheaval.inYou: Holy discontent may rupture your comfortable arrangement and send you somewhere you never trained for. The break can fall on an utterly ordinary person — no credentials, no platform, mid-life and mid-career — carrying a word that, once you have spoken it, will not be unheard. Do not disqualify yourself. The herdsman did not qualify either, and God took him anyway.
upheaval.inTheBody: A comfortable, prosperous church is exactly the kind of thing God has ruptured before. Amos shows the disconnect aimed straight at religion grown fat and unjust — full festivals, empty justice, songs God says He cannot bear. Renewal here is the prophetic break that calls a complacent people off their crowded worship and back to righteousness rolling down like a river.
upheaval.whatRemains: Beneath the ruptured festivals stands the God who would rather have justice than songs. What cannot be shaken is His unchanging character — righteousness that rolls down like waters, mercy that outlasts every liturgy. The worship He hates can be stripped away entirely, and the just and living God it failed to honor remains, still calling His people home.
reflection: Where has a holy discontent been disturbing my comfortable arrangement, and have I treated it as enemy or as call?
What disqualification am I hiding behind to avoid the word God may be putting in my mouth?
Has my worship drifted from my justice — full festivals on one day, forgotten poor on the next?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have loved the comfortable festival and forgotten the justice You actually want. Rupture my settled religion if You must. Take away the noise of my songs, and let righteousness roll down through my life like a river. Send me where You will; I have no credentials but Your call. Amen.

notes.primary: Amos 5:24 (let justice roll down); Amos 7:14-15 (the herdsman called from the flock).

title: How can I give you up?
moment: Hosea is told to do a strange and costly thing: marry a woman who will break his heart, and let the marriage become a sermon. His private grief over an unfaithful wife is made into a window onto God's grief over an unfaithful people. We brace for the verdict to fall — surely the next word is divorce, abandonment, the door shut for good. Instead comes a line that turns the whole picture inside out. I will allure her, the LORD says, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak tenderly there. The coming disconnect is not a cold dismissal. It is a courtship. He means to lead her out, away from the crowd and the other lovers, into a place quiet enough that she can hear Him again. And then, in chapter eleven, the mask of the wronged husband slips and the raw heart underneath shows through: how can I give you up? The compassion is stirred; the heart recoils at the very thought of letting her go. Even when God breaks with His people, He is not breaking free of them. He is breaking through to them.
voiceQuote: Behold, I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak comfortably to her.
scriptureText: How shall I give you up, Ephraim?... my heart is turned within me, my compassion is aroused.
weight: We read every wilderness as punishment. The relationship cools, the comfort is withdrawn, the familiar securities fall away, and we conclude that we are being discarded — that the silence is the sound of a God who has finally had enough. Hosea will not let that reading stand. The wilderness here is not a sentence; it is a strategy of love. He leads the beloved out precisely because He wants her back, and the only way to be heard over the noise of all the lesser loves is to get her alone. So if your upheaval has stripped your life down to a quiet you did not ask for, do not be so sure it is rejection. The God who breaks with you is not the God who is finished with you. His heart is turned within Him even as He leads you out. The very emptiness that feels like abandonment may be the space He has cleared so that, for the first time in a long while, you can hear Him speak tenderly to your heart.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect can be the work of love, not its withdrawal. This break is a wilderness with a purpose: to get the beloved alone. The phase asks you to consider that the rupture aiming you toward emptiness may be a courtship in disguise, a clearing made so the One who broke with you can speak.
upheaval.inYou: If God has led you into a wilderness, weigh the possibility that it is the strange courtship of love and not the cold of rejection. The break may be exactly how He gets you alone, away from the noise and the rival loves, to speak to your heart again in a voice you had stopped being able to hear.
upheaval.inTheBody: God's disciplining break with a wayward church is not the act of a God who is done with her. His heart is turned within Him; His compassion is stirred. He breaks in order to allure, and He allures in order to win her back. A community led into its wilderness is being courted, not cast off.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the love that authors even the break. His compassion does not cool when His people wander; His heart recoils at giving them up. The wilderness can be removed; the relentless tenderness that led you into it remains.
reflection: Have I been reading my wilderness as rejection when it might be a courtship?
What lesser loves has this emptiness quietly cleared away so I could hear God again?
Can I believe that the One who broke with me still cannot bear to give me up?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, this wilderness has felt like You walking away. Show me it is You leading me out to speak tenderly, away from every other voice. I had grown deaf in the noise. Let me hear You here, and trust the love behind the break. Amen.

notes.primary: Hosea 2:14 (I will allure her into the wilderness); Hosea 11:8 (how shall I give you up?).

title: Here am I; send me
moment: Isaiah's call does not begin with a commission. It begins with a collapse. In the year the king dies, the temple fills with a vision too large for the room: the LORD high and lifted up, the train of His robe flooding the floor, the seraphim crying holy, holy, holy until the doorposts shake and the house fills with smoke. And the first thing out of the prophet's mouth is not eagerness but horror. Woe is me, he says, for I am undone. The vision has not flattered him; it has unmade him. A man of unclean lips, dwelling among a people of unclean lips, and now his eyes have seen the King. Only after that — after a coal from the altar touches his mouth and the guilt is taken away — does he hear the question, whom shall I send? The undone, cleansed man can finally answer it: here am I; send me. Notice the order, because it never changes. The vision of God breaks the old self apart before it ever hands the new self its work. Isaiah is unraveled in the holy presence, and only then is he sent.
voiceQuote: I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then I said, Here am I; send me.
scriptureText: Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips... for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of Hosts.
weight: We want our callings to arrive as affirmation — confirmation that we are competent, ready, fit for the task. But a true encounter with the holiness of God does not affirm you first; it undoes you first. It shows you, against the blazing purity of the One on the throne, exactly how much of your self-assurance was never silver. And that undoing is not a detour around your vocation. It is the doorway into it. The man who has not been brought to woe is me is not yet ready to be trusted with here am I, because he will go in his own strength and on his own authority, and that is precisely the thing the vision burns away. So if your upheaval has stripped you of the confidence you used to lead with — if you feel more undone than equipped — do not read that as disqualification. The unraveling before the holy God is the very thing that fits you to be sent. Woe is me comes first, and it is supposed to.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect is the breaking of the old self that must precede any sending. This phase asks you to let the encounter undo you before it commissions you — to stop bracing for affirmation and let the vision of God dismantle your self-sufficiency, because only the undone and cleansed are finally fit to go.
upheaval.inYou: A true encounter with God's holiness undoes you before it ever sends you. The breaking of your self-sufficiency is not an interruption of your calling; it is the very way in. Do not despise the unraveling, and do not mistake it for disqualification. Woe is me comes before here am I, and the order is mercy, not cruelty.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church that has genuinely seen God is first undone by Him, then commissioned. Renewal that skips the woe — the honest unraveling before the holy God — sends no one anywhere worth going. The break precedes the sending in the body too; a people unmade in His presence are the only ones fit to be sent from it.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the holiness that undoes you and the grace that cleanses you. Your self-assurance is burned away, but the coal still comes from the altar; the guilt is still taken. The One on the throne remains, and so does His sending word.
reflection: Has my upheaval undone my self-sufficiency — and can I receive that as the doorway to calling, not the end of it?
Am I waiting for affirmation when God means first to bring me to woe is me?
What has the vision of His holiness shown me about what in me was never silver?
upheaval.prayer: Holy God, I came looking for affirmation and You have undone me instead. I am a person of unclean lips, and my eyes have seen the King. Touch me with the coal from Your altar, take the guilt away, and only then send me. Amen.

notes.primary: Isaiah 6:8 (here am I, send me); Isaiah 6:5 (woe is me, I am undone).

title: Don't say, I am a child
moment: The word of the LORD breaks into a young man's settled life, and it does not ease in gently. Before you were born, God says, I knew you; I set you apart; I appointed you a prophet to the nations. It is a staggering thing to be handed, and Jeremiah does what almost all of us do when the call outruns our sense of ourselves. He reaches for the nearest excuse. Ah, Lord GOD, he says, I cannot speak, for I am only a child. It is not false modesty; he means it. He is too young, untried, unready, and he holds his disqualification up like a shield. God brushes it aside on the spot. Do not say, I am a child. To whomever I send you, you shall go; whatever I command you, you shall speak. And then, knowing the real fear underneath the excuse, He adds the only assurance that actually matters: do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you. The break does not wait for Jeremiah to feel ready. It rests on a different ground entirely — not the prophet's competence, but God's presence.
voiceQuote: Don't say, I am a child; for to whoever I shall send you, you shall go, and whatever I shall command you, you shall speak.
scriptureText: Don't be afraid because of them; for I am with you to deliver you, says the LORD.
weight: When God calls you out of the familiar, you will reach for your disqualification, and you will have a real one ready. Too young or too old, too broken, too compromised, too untrained, too tired, too late. The excuse is not always a lie; Jeremiah really was young. But notice that God does not argue him into feeling adequate. He does not list Jeremiah's hidden talents or promise that he will grow into the role and feel confident soon. He simply overrides the excuse with a presence. The readiness the call requires was never your readiness; it was His being with you. This is bracing and it is freeing at once. Bracing, because it means you do not get to wait until you feel equal to the thing before you obey it — that day may never come. Freeing, because the weight you thought rested on your competence was never yours to carry. The break comes to the reluctant and the unready, and the only qualification it asks for is the One who promises to go along.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect often comes to the reluctant, and it does not honor our excuses. This phase asks you to stop hiding behind your disqualification and to move on different ground entirely — not your readiness, which may never arrive, but God's promise to be with you. The excuse is rarely accepted; the presence is always given.
upheaval.inYou: When God calls you out, you will reach for your disqualification — too young, too old, too broken, not trained, not ready. The break does not wait for your sense of readiness, because that ground is sand. It rests on something firmer: His promise to be with you to deliver you.
upheaval.inTheBody: God keeps raising up renewers who feel utterly unqualified for the rupture they are handed. The church's great breaks have often come through reluctant people who said, in effect, I am only a child — and then went anyway, because the One who sent them had promised to go with them.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the presence promised to the called: I am with you to deliver you. Your competence can fail and your courage can drain away, but the assurance underneath the call does not move. He goes with the ones He sends.
reflection: What disqualification am I holding up like a shield when God calls me out?
Have I been waiting to feel ready, on ground that may never grow firm?
Can I move on His promise to be with me rather than on my own sense of competence?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, when You call me I reach for every reason I am not the one. I am too young, too small, too unready. Do not let me hide there. Steady me on the only ground that holds: that You are with me to deliver me. I will go because You go with me. Amen.

notes.primary: Jeremiah 1:7-8 (don't say I am a child; I am with you).

title: The voice in the wilderness
moment: John comes from outside everything. Not from the temple courts or the priestly schools but from the wilderness, dressed in camel hair, eating locusts and wild honey, a living rupture in the religious landscape. The crowds stream out to the Jordan to be baptized by him, confessing their sins, and the whole settled machinery of holiness — the right place, the right lineage, the right offerings — is quietly bypassed by a man preparing a road through the desert. He is the voice crying in the wilderness, the one Isaiah foretold: make ready the way of the Lord, make His paths straight. And then comes the most astonishing thing about him, the thing that sets him apart from every demagogue who ever drew a crowd. When his own followers fret that Jesus is baptizing and everyone is going to Him, John does not cling to his moment. He answers with joy. He must increase, John says, but I must decrease. The forerunner breaks the old order open, prepares the way for One greater, and then deliberately, gladly, steps out of it. His whole vocation was to point past himself and then to shrink so the Light behind him could be seen.
voiceQuote: The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Make ready the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.
voiceAttribution: Isaiah, of John the Baptist — Matthew 3:3 (WEB)
scriptureText: He must increase, but I must decrease.
weight: Some breaks are not about you arriving. They are about you preparing a way for something far larger than yourself — and then getting out of its way. This is the hardest kind of disconnect, because it asks you to do real, rupturing, costly work and then to let it be eclipsed. To pour your life into clearing a road and then watch the traffic pass you by toward Someone else, and to call that joy. John shows us a self that is held so lightly it can decrease without panic. He had every ingredient of a movement built around him — the crowds, the loyalty, the moral authority — and he spent it all pointing away from himself. So when your part in God's work turns out to be the forerunner's part, the voice and not the Word, the one who prepares and then recedes, do not grasp. The disconnect was never finally about your prominence or your platform. It was about clearing a path and pointing past yourself to the One who comes after, who is greater, and who must increase.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect sometimes makes you a forerunner — the one who ruptures the old order and then points past himself. This phase asks for a self held lightly enough to decrease, to do the breaking work of preparing a way and then, without grasping, to step aside so the greater thing can be seen.
upheaval.inYou: Some breaks call you to prepare a way for something far larger than yourself — and then to decrease. The disconnect is not finally about your prominence or your platform; it is about clearing a path and pointing past yourself to the One who comes after you, and learning to call your own shrinking joy.
upheaval.inTheBody: Renewal movements are often forerunners — voices in the wilderness preparing a way, called to decrease once the larger work arrives. The church needs its John the Baptists: those willing to rupture the old order, point past themselves, and then, gladly, step aside so the One they announced can increase.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the One the forerunner points to — the increasing Christ. Platforms rise and recede, voices are raised and then fall silent, but He must increase. The decreasing self loses nothing real, because what remains is the Light it was only ever clearing the way for.
reflection: Where is God asking me to prepare a way and then to decrease?
Am I clinging to a prominence that was only ever meant to point past itself?
Can I call it joy when the work I poured myself into is eclipsed by Someone greater?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I want to arrive, and You are asking me to prepare a way and then to fade. Teach me John's strange joy: that You must increase and I must decrease. Hold my small self loosely in Your hand. Let me point past myself to You, and be glad. Amen.

notes.primary: Matthew 3:3 (the voice crying in the wilderness); John 3:30 (he must increase, I must decrease).

title: They left their nets
moment: Jesus walks the shore of Galilee and sees two brothers, Simon and Andrew, casting a net into the sea, because they were fishermen. It is an ordinary morning of ordinary work. He says two words — come after me — and adds a promise that turns their whole trade into a metaphor: I will make you into fishers for men. And then Mark writes the word that ought to stop us in our tracks. Immediately. Immediately they left the nets and followed Him. Not after the season's catch was in. Not after they had trained a replacement, settled the accounts, talked it over with their father, weighed what they would gain against what they would lose. The nets, their income, their identity as fishermen, the whole shape of the life they had built — dropped on the sand where they stood. A little farther on it happens again: James and John, mending nets in the boat with their father Zebedee, and at the call they leave the boat and the old man and the hired hands and go. There is no transition plan in the story. There is only a call, and an immediate, total yes.
voiceQuote: Come after me, and I will make you into fishers for men.
scriptureText: Immediately they left their nets, and followed him.
weight: We are fond of the cushioned obedience — the call we can plan around, schedule, fund, and ease into so gently that it costs us no sleep and no security. And much of the time God does work slowly, and wisdom does count the cost. But Mark's immediately stands there as a warning against turning every call into a committee. Because now and then the call is unmistakable, and the only faithful answer is the immediate one. The nets have to go down on the sand, today, before you are ready, before the season is finished, before you have talked yourself into a more comfortable version of obedience. Some disconnects cannot be cushioned and scheduled and managed; they can only be obeyed. The danger is not that you will move too fast. The danger is the slow erosion of the capacity to move at all — the soul so practiced at counting costs that it can no longer simply rise and follow. When the call is clear, the most dangerous thing you can do is wait until it is convenient.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect can be instant — a call that breaks a life open in a single moment and is answered before it can be talked away. This phase asks for a readiness to obey the unmistakable call immediately, to drop the nets where you stand rather than schedule the leaving for a season that suits you better.
upheaval.inYou: Now and then the call is unmistakable, and the only faithful response is the immediate one — to drop the nets and go. Not every disconnect can be planned, cushioned, and neatly scheduled for later. Some must simply be obeyed, today, before you have quietly managed to talk yourself out of them.
upheaval.inTheBody: The church is built on people who dropped their nets. A community that has wholly lost the capacity for the immediate, total yes has lost something of its very founding. The call still comes; the nets, sooner or later, still have to be left on the sand, before the season is convenient.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the Caller and the promise He attaches to the leaving: I will make you into fishers for men. The nets are dropped and the old identity falls away, but the One who issued the call remains, and so does the new making He has in mind.
reflection: Is there a call I have heard clearly and kept scheduling for a more convenient season?
Have I turned obedience into a committee that can no longer simply rise and follow?
What nets would I have to drop today if I truly answered the call I have already heard?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I am skilled at the cushioned yes, the obedience I can plan and postpone. When Your call is unmistakable, do not let me wait for convenience. Give me the courage of the fishermen, to leave the nets where I stand and follow before I argue myself out of it. Amen.

notes.primary: Mark 1:17-18 (come after me; immediately they left their nets).

title: The cost of following
moment:
A scribe runs up, full of zeal, and offers Jesus the most generous thing a man can say: I will follow you wherever you go. It is exactly the response a teacher might want, and Jesus does not seize it. Instead He tells the truth about the road. The foxes have their dens and the birds of the sky have their nests, He says, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay His head. Follow Me, and you follow a man with no pillow of His own. There will be no settled address, no soft landing at the end of the day.

Then another would-be disciple asks for one reasonable delay first: let me go and bury my father. It is not a frivolous request; it is duty, family, the most sacred of obligations. And Jesus answers with a hard word that has unsettled readers ever since: leave the dead to bury their own dead. The sayings sting because the break is genuinely costly. He will not dress it up, will not sell a discipleship with all the comforts left intact. The disconnect is real, and He refuses to pretend it is cheap.
voiceQuote: The foxes have holes, and the birds of the sky have nests, but the Son of Man has no place to lay his head.
scriptureText: Follow me, and leave the dead to bury their own dead.
weight:
We like to count the cost of following the way we count the price of a thing we mean to buy anyway, expecting the number to be manageable. Jesus will not cooperate. He tells you the break will cost more than you budgeted: the security you assumed you could keep, the comfortable delay you were sure was reasonable, the obligation that quietly hardens into an excuse. He says it out loud before you pay, which is its own kind of mercy.

The honesty is not meant to frighten you off. It is meant to make your yes a real yes, given with open eyes, so it can survive the homelessness it walks into. A following that was sold to you as costless would collapse the first night there was no place to lay your head. Better to hear the price now, in the daylight, from the One who has already paid more of it than you ever will. He names the cost so the disconnect, when it comes, does not feel like a betrayal of the promise. It was the promise.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect names the price before you pay it. The phase asks you to leave with your eyes open, counting what the break will actually cost rather than what you hoped it might: the security, the delay, the obligation turned excuse. It refuses to sell you a costless following, and having named the homelessness, it still says, follow.
upheaval.inYou: The break will cost more than you set aside for it. Some security you meant to keep, some reasonable delay, some duty that has quietly become a place to hide. Jesus tells you the truth about the price not to scare you off, but so the yes you give is real enough to walk into the homelessness and not turn back.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church that advertises a costless following grows shallow disciples and brittle communities, ready to scatter the first hard night. The honest call names the homelessness and the severed ties at the outset. A body willing to say the price out loud, and to follow anyway, builds something that holds when the soft landing never comes.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is not the address you lose but the One you follow. Houses and nests and soft landings all give way; the Son of Man who had nowhere to lay His head is Himself the resting place that remains when every other shelter is gone.
reflection: What did the break cost that I had not budgeted for, and am I still resenting the bill?
Which reasonable delay have I let harden into an excuse to keep from following?
Is my yes to Christ a real yes, given with open eyes, or one I assumed would stay comfortable?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, You never sold me a costless following, and I am grateful now for the honesty. Where the break has cost more than I planned, steady me. Make my yes a real yes, eyes open, willing for the homelessness, because You are the only resting place I finally need. Amen.

notes.primary: Luke 9:58 (foxes have holes); Matthew 8:22 (leave the dead to bury their own dead).

title: The break he would not make
moment:
A man comes running and falls on his knees in the road, and everything about him is right. He is earnest, he is moral, he is hungry for more than he has: good teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life? He has kept the commandments since he was a boy, and he is not lying. And then comes the line that turns the whole scene tender and terrible at once. Jesus, looking at him, loved him. Into that love He speaks the single break the man cannot make: you lack one thing; go, sell what you have, give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow Me.

The air goes out of the encounter. His face falls. He had come for a teacher's blessing on a life already mostly built, and instead he is handed the one demand that touches the thing he cannot release. He goes away grieving, because he had great possessions. Read it again and the grief reverses: not because he had them, but because they had him. It may be the saddest sentence in the Gospels. The disconnect was right there in front of him, named by Love itself, and he would not make it.
voiceQuote: One thing you lack: go, sell whatever you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.
voiceAttribution: Jesus, to the rich young man — Mark 10:21 (WEB)
scriptureText: But his face fell at that saying, and he went away sorrowful, for he was one who had great possessions.
weight:
There is usually one thing you will not put down, and it is almost always the very thing that has its hand around you. You can tell which it is by how quickly you reach for reasons. The break you keep declining, the one you have a dozen good arguments against, is often the exact one God has been naming all along. Everything else you would surrender; this you defend.

What makes the story so sobering is that the man does nothing scandalous. He does not curse, does not storm off, does not deny the faith. He simply keeps what he came in with and walks away sad. You can do that. You can leave the encounter with your possessions intact, your morality intact, your sincerity intact, and miss the one thing you actually came for. The disconnect was within reach and you chose, gently and grievously, to keep what owned you. The tragedy of the refused break is not that it is dramatic. It is that it looks so reasonable, and leaves you exactly where you were, only sadder.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect sometimes is the break refused. The phase exposes the one possession that turns out to own you, and asks you to release it. Here it is declined: the man keeps what he holds and walks away grieving. The cost of the refused break is to remain correct, sincere, and unchanged, sorrowful on the far side of the very door you would not walk through.
upheaval.inYou: There may be one thing you will not release, and it is usually the thing that owns you. The break you keep declining is often the exact one God is asking for. Be honest about which it is. You can walk away with everything intact, sincere and sorrowful, and miss the one thing you came kneeling in the road to find.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church can be the rich young ruler: doctrinally sound, genuinely seeking, and quietly unwilling to release the one thing Christ keeps naming, whether its wealth, its status, or its control. The refused break leaves a community correct and comfortable and grieving, mostly built and unchanged, walking away from the very Love that named the one thing it lacked.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the treasure in heaven the man would not trade for. Possessions own us and then slip our grip in the end regardless; the treasure Christ offers in exchange for the break is the one holding that no loss can reach and no refusal can finally cancel.
reflection: What is the one thing I will not release, and has it begun to own me?
Which break do I have the most reasons against, and is that the very one being asked?
Could I walk away sincere and unchanged, keeping everything and missing the one thing I came for?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, You see the one thing I keep defending, and we both know it has its hand on me. I have a dozen reasons; You have one word. Give me the grace to put it down and come, rather than walk away intact and grieving. Let nothing own me but You. Amen.

notes.primary: Mark 10:21-22 (the one thing he lacked; he went away sorrowful).

title: Zacchaeus comes down
moment:
Set this little man beside the one who walked away, and the whole phase comes into focus. Zacchaeus is a chief tax collector, rich the way the rich young ruler was rich, and despised for how he got it. He is too short to see over the crowd, so he does an undignified thing for a man of his standing: he runs ahead and climbs a sycamore tree like a child. And Jesus, passing under it, stops, looks up, and calls him down by name to dinner. Grace gets to him first, before a single demand is made.

What follows is not a sorrowful face but a standing-up. Zacchaeus rises, there in his own house, and announces it gladly: behold, Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor, and if I have cheated anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold. No one twisted his arm. The release that crushed the rich young ruler reads here like joy, almost like relief, a man unburdening himself of what he had spent his life grasping. Same wealth, opposite response. And Jesus names what has happened: today salvation has come to this house. Same disconnect, entirely different heart.
voiceQuote: Behold, Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much.
scriptureText: Today, salvation has come to this house.
weight:
The release you dread can arrive as gladness when grace reaches you before the demand does. This is the hinge the two stories turn on. The rich young ruler met the requirement first and the love underneath it second, and the weight crushed him. Zacchaeus was sought out, called down by name, welcomed before he had reformed a thing, and the letting-go came easy, almost as relief. The break did not change; the order did.

So if you have been white-knuckling your way toward generosity, gritting your teeth to pry your own fingers loose, it may be that you are trying to make the break before you have let the grace land. Zacchaeus did not grind out his fourfold restitution as a grim duty. He was found, and being found, he could not give it away fast enough. Grace has a way of making the costly disconnect feel less like amputation and more like freedom, less like loss and more like setting down a weight you were tired of carrying. The same release that breaks one heart, when grace goes first, liberates another.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect can be the break made gladly. The same release that crushed one man here liberates another, because grace arrived first. The phase still asks for the letting-go, the open hand, the wealth given away. But when grace gets there ahead of the demand, the break stops feeling like amputation and starts feeling like freedom, given with joy rather than grief.
upheaval.inYou: The release you dread can come as joy when grace reaches you first. Zacchaeus did not white-knuckle his way to generosity; he was found, sought out by name, and the letting-go came gladly, almost as relief. If the break feels like pure loss, ask whether you are trying to make it before you have let the grace that makes it light actually land.
upheaval.inTheBody: A community gripped by grace releases its securities gladly rather than grudgingly. When a church gives, sends, and lets go and it feels like freedom instead of amputation, that is the Zacchaeus break. The body that has been found does not grit its teeth over its generosity; it can scarcely give fast enough, and salvation, Jesus says, has come to the house.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the salvation that came to the house. Goods given away are gone, and gladly so; but the One who called Zacchaeus down by name and sat at his table is the abiding thing, the presence that turned a costly release into joy and remains when the wealth is happily spent.
reflection: Am I trying to make a break before I have let the grace that lightens it reach me?
Where have I been white-knuckling a release that grace could make glad?
What have I grasped so long that letting it go would feel less like loss and more like relief?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, You sought me out and called me down by name before I had set one thing right. Let that grace land deep enough that the releases I dread become freedom. Loosen my grip gladly, not grimly, and let me give like a man unburdened. Come to this house today. Amen.

notes.primary: Luke 19:8-9 (Zacchaeus gives half his goods; salvation comes to his house).

title: Overturning the tables
moment:
Here is holy discontent in the flesh, and it is holding a whip of cords. Jesus comes into the temple and finds the outer court turned into a bazaar: tables of money changers, pens of oxen and sheep, cages of doves, the clink of coins where there should have been the murmur of prayer. The one place set apart for the nations to seek God has been made a marketplace on holy ground. And He does not negotiate. He overturns the tables, drives out the animals, scatters the coins across the stones, and says it plainly: take these out of here; do not make My Father's house a market.

In the other telling He sharpens it. This house was meant to be called a house of prayer for all the nations, and you have made it a den of robbers. Notice what the break is aimed at. Not at worship, which He is fierce to protect, but at the corruption that had crowded worship out. This is the disconnect turned squarely against religion gone rotten, the violent clearing of what had defiled the holy. The whip is not the destruction of the temple. It is the cleansing of it. And the discontent driving it is His, and it is holy.
voiceQuote: Take these things out of here. Don't make my Father's house a marketplace.
scriptureText: My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations; but you have made it a den of robbers.
weight:
There are tables in you that need overturning, and you can usually feel where they stand. They are the places where something that began as worship has quietly curdled into a transaction: prayer that has become a way to get, devotion that has become a performance, the sacred turned into a means to an end. The marketplace does not announce itself. It creeps in by the booth, one small concession at a time, until the house of prayer is doing a brisk trade.

When the disruption comes that flips those tables, the instinct is to flinch, to call it loss, to mourn the booth. Welcome it instead. The One scattering your coins is not a vandal in the temple; He is its rightful Lord, and He is clearing the house, not wrecking it. The cleansing break feels violent because the corruption had grown comfortable, learned to look like part of the furniture. What the whip ends is far worse than the whip. A heart should fear the marketplace it has made of the holy place far more than the cords that drive the market out.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect is here Jesus' own holy discontent, overturning a corrupted system. The phase is the violent clearing of what has defiled the holy, aimed not at worship but at the marketplace that crowded worship out. It asks you to welcome the disruption rather than mourn the booth, and to trust that the One flipping the tables is cleansing the house.
upheaval.inYou: There are tables in you that need overturning, the places where something sacred has quietly become a transaction, a performance, a way to get. Welcome the disruption when it comes. The One flipping those tables is not vandalizing the house; He is cleansing it. Fear the marketplace you have made of the holy far more than the cords that clear it.
upheaval.inTheBody: When a church has made the Father's house a marketplace, selling access, trading on God, monetizing the holy, the cleansing break is mercy and not cruelty. Christ still overturns tables. A community should fear the corruption that crept in by the booth far more than the whip that clears it, and should welcome the Lord who comes to cleanse His own house.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the house of prayer for all the nations, the thing the marketplace had buried. Tables overturn and coins scatter and the booth is driven out; what remains when the cleansing is done is the holy purpose the corruption had crowded out, standing clear again at last.
reflection: What in me began as worship and has quietly curdled into a way to get something?
Which booth in my holy place have I let creep in until it looks like the furniture?
Do I fear the disruption that would cleanse me more than the corruption that needs cleansing?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have let a marketplace creep into the house meant for prayer, one small booth at a time. Come in with the cords. Overturn the tables where I made the sacred a transaction, and do not spare the booth I have grown fond of. Cleanse the house. It is Yours, not mine. Amen.

notes.primary: John 2:16 (don't make my Father's house a marketplace); Mark 11:17 (a house of prayer made a den of robbers).

title: Not peace, but a sword
moment:
It is one of the hardest things Jesus ever says, and He says it without flinching: do not think that I came to bring peace on the earth; I did not come to bring peace, but a sword. To ears that have learned to call Him only gentle, it lands wrong. He goes on to spell out where the sword falls, and it is not on some distant battlefield. It falls at the kitchen table. A man set against his father, a daughter against her mother, a household divided against itself. The blade runs straight through the family.

Luke records the same hard saying. Do you suppose I came to give peace on the earth? No, He says, but rather division. And the meaning is not that Jesus delights in conflict, nor that the gospel has failed when it splits a room. It is that allegiance to Him reorders every other loyalty a person holds, and that reordering can crack a family down its center. The gospel that is peace with God often brings, among people who must now decide where Christ ranks, a sword. The break the gospel causes is not a malfunction of the gospel. Sometimes it is the gospel doing precisely what the gospel does.
voiceQuote: Don't think that I came to send peace on the earth. I didn't come to send peace, but a sword.
scriptureText: Do you think that I have come to give peace in the earth? I tell you, no, but rather division.
weight:
Following Christ may divide you from people you love, and you will be tempted to read that division as proof you have done something wrong. You did not go looking for conflict. But the new allegiance has quietly reordered all the old ones, and the people who counted on the old ranking can feel the floor shift, and some of them will not forgive it. The sword falls, and it falls grievously, between you and faces you have loved your whole life.

Hear what Jesus is doing by saying it out loud. He is refusing to let the break catch you unprepared. He will not send you into the kitchen with a promise of easy peace and let you conclude, when the division comes, that your faith has failed. He names the sword in advance so that, when it falls, you do not mistake it for your own fault or for God's absence. The grief is real; He does not minimize it. But the division is not the enemy of peace. It is the blade that clears the ground where a deeper peace, the kind that starts with God, can finally take root.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect includes the division the gospel itself creates, even at the kitchen table. The phase names a break you did not choose and cannot prevent: allegiance to Christ reorders every loyalty, and the reordering can split a household. It asks you to receive the sword not as the gospel failing, but as the gospel doing exactly what, sometimes, the gospel does.
upheaval.inYou: Following Christ may divide you from people you love, not because you went looking for conflict but because the new allegiance reorders all the old ones. That sword is grievous. Jesus named it plainly so the break would not catch you unprepared, and so you would not mistake the division for your own failure or doubt your faith the moment it falls.
upheaval.inTheBody: The gospel's advance has always divided even as it gathered. A church should not be naive: faithfulness will create breaks, with the surrounding culture, sometimes within families and even congregations. The sword is not the enemy of peace. It clears the ground where a deeper peace can grow, and a body braced for the division will not read it as proof the gospel has failed.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the peace with God the sword was never aimed at. Human loyalties realign and households crack; the reconciliation Christ won between you and the Father stands underneath the division, the deeper peace the blade clears ground for and never touches.
reflection: Where has following Christ divided me from people I love, and have I read it as my failure?
Which old loyalty has my new allegiance reordered, and who feels the floor shifting?
Can I hold the grief of the sword and still trust the deeper peace it clears ground for?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, the sword has fallen where I least wanted it, between me and people I love, and I have wondered if I failed. You named it before it came so I would not mistake it for Your absence. Hold me in the grief, and root me in the deeper peace with God that the blade was never aimed against. Amen.

notes.primary: Matthew 10:34 (not peace but a sword); Luke 12:51 (division, not peace).

title: Not my will
moment: The deepest disconnect in Scripture happens on the ground, in a garden, in the dark. He kneels among the olive trees, and the sweat comes down like falling blood, and He prays the most human prayer there is: Father, if you are willing, take this cup from me. He does not want it. He says so plainly, and He says it more than once. There is no pretending here, no manufactured calm. He asks for the cup to pass because He honestly wishes it would. And then, in the same breath, He makes the break that every other break in the world only rehearses. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done. He hands over the one thing a person clings to hardest — the wanting itself, the preference, the plan — while the wanting is still alive and aching in His chest. To surrender your own will, not after it has gone quiet but while it is still crying out, is the hardest rupture a human heart can make. He made it first. He made it in the dark, on the ground, and He made it for us.
voiceQuote: Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.
scriptureText: My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me; nevertheless, not what I want, but what you want.
weight: The break God asks of you may not be from a possession or a place or a person. It may be from your own will — the plan you have built your hope on, the preference you cannot seem to lay down, the outcome you are still aching for in the middle of the night. We imagine surrender as a kind of peace that descends and quiets the wanting first. Gethsemane says otherwise. You can want the cup gone with your whole body and still pray that His will be done. The honesty and the obedience are not enemies; they belong together on the same ground. You do not have to feel serene to be faithful, and you do not have to stop wishing for another way in order to say yours be done. The raw asking is not a failure of trust. It is what real surrender looks like before it is finished — a heart that tells God the truth about what it wants, and hands the wanting over anyway.

upheaval.thePhase: This is Disconnect at its most interior: the break not from something you hold but from your own will. The phase asks what every garden asks — that you release your grip on the outcome while the longing for it is still raw, praying not my will but yours, and meaning it without pretending the cup is easy.
upheaval.inYou: The break before you may be from your own will — your plan, your preference, the ending you keep rehearsing in hope. Gethsemane shows you can want the cup gone and still pray yours be done. You need not fake serenity to obey. Tell God the truth about what you want, and hand the wanting over in the same prayer.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church discerning God's will must sometimes break from its own — its preferred future, its institutional self-interest, the survival instinct that masquerades as faithfulness. The Gethsemane prayer, prayed by a whole body, is costly: not our will but yours, even when the community can see plainly what obedience is going to cost it, and chooses obedience anyway.
upheaval.whatRemains: When your own will is finally broken, what does not break is the Father into whose hands the will is given. The wanting can be shaken loose; His good purpose underneath it cannot. That is what remains when surrender has cost you everything — not your plan, but the One who held you while you let it go.
reflection: What cup am I still asking God to take from me, and can I pray yours be done in the same breath?
Where have I mistaken raw honesty about my wants for a lack of faith?
What would it look like to hand over my own will while it is still aching, rather than waiting to feel calm first?
upheaval.prayer: Father, there is a cup I do not want, and I will not pretend otherwise. I have asked You to take it, and I ask again. And still, in the same breath, I give You my will: not what I want, but what You want. Hold me while I let it go. Amen.

notes.primary: Luke 22:42 / Matthew 26:39 (not my will but yours, in Gethsemane).

title: It is finished
moment: The cross is the ultimate disconnect, and it speaks two words that should not be able to live in the same hour. The first is desolation. Out of the darkness over the whole land comes the most forsaken cry ever uttered: my God, my God, why have you forsaken me. The communion at the very center of reality — the Son with the Father, before all worlds — seems, for one unbearable moment, to tear. There is no softening this. He is not performing abandonment; He is in it. And then, from the same cross, in the same dying, comes the other word, and it is not a word of defeat. It is finished. Not I am finished, not it is over and lost, but the work is done, accomplished, complete. The thing He came to do has been carried all the way through to the end. So the deepest rupture the universe has ever known is, at the very same instant, its deepest completion. The tearing and the finishing are one act. What looks from below like the end of everything is, from the cross itself, the accomplishing of everything.
voiceQuote: When Jesus had received the vinegar, he said, It is finished. He bowed his head, and gave up his spirit.
scriptureText: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?
weight: When your own forsakenness is at its worst — when God seems to have torn Himself away and left you alone in the dark, when the prayers go up and nothing comes back down — the cross does not hand you an explanation. It hands you a companion. Even that desolation has been entered, borne all the way to the bottom, and turned into finished work. There is no abandonment you can feel that He has not already felt ahead of you. He went into the God-forsaken dark first, and He came out the other side calling it accomplished. So when you cannot sense Him, the question is not whether He is real but whether your feeling is the final word. It is not. The cross says the worst hour you will ever live was walked through by the Son, and on its far side stands a word you cannot yet say but He has already spoken over it: finished. The dark is not the end of the story. It is finished is.

upheaval.thePhase: This is Disconnect at its furthest reach — the Son forsaken, the rupture total. Yet the phase reveals its secret here: the very same break is the work completed. Disconnect asks you to trust that even the bottom, even the dark where God seems gone, can be the place where something is finished rather than the place where you are.
upheaval.inYou: When you feel most God-forsaken — torn from, left in the dark, sure He has gone — the cross says even that has been entered ahead of you and turned into finished work. There is no abandonment you can feel that He has not already walked through, all the way down. Your dark is not outside His story; He has been to the bottom of it first.
upheaval.inTheBody: The church's darkest hours, when it feels utterly God-forsaken and stripped of everything it leaned on, are not outside the pattern of its Lord. The cross stands at the center of the faith precisely as the disconnect that accomplished everything. A community in the dark has not fallen out of the story. Forsakenness is not the end of it. It is finished is.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the finished work itself. Feelings of abandonment come and go; the cry in the dark is real and then it passes. But what was accomplished on that cross is done, and nothing can undo it. When everything else is torn away, the completed work of Christ remains, finished and unshakable.
reflection: Where do I feel most forsaken right now, and have I let that feeling become the final word?
Can I believe that Christ has already walked through the exact dark I am in?
What changes if the worst hour of my life is met not by an explanation but by a finished work?
upheaval.prayer: Lord Jesus, in the dark I have wondered if You forsook me. You know that cry; You made it first. Thank You that even my forsakenness has been entered and borne by You. When I cannot feel You, hold me to the word You finished over it: it is done. Amen.

notes.primary: John 19:30 (it is finished); Matthew 27:46 (my God, my God, why have you forsaken me).

title: The veil is torn
moment: At the very moment He dies, something tears in a building across the city. The veil of the temple, the thick curtain that walled off the holiest place, rips in two from top to bottom. The direction matters. It is not torn from the bottom up, as if human hands had finally reached high enough to pull it down. It tears from the top, from God's end, His doing and not ours. For generations that curtain had done its work, keeping everyone out of the place where God was said to dwell, admitting only one man one day a year, and only with blood. Now, in an instant, it hangs open. This is disconnect as doorway. The whole old system of separation comes to an end, and through the very place it tears, a new and living way opens straight into the presence no one could approach before. Hebrews would later say the way leads through the veil, that is, through His flesh — the curtain and the body torn in the same hour, for the same reason. Sometimes the breaking of the old order is the exact thing that grants an access no one ever had while it stood.
voiceQuote: The veil of the temple was torn in two from the top to the bottom.
voiceAttribution: Mark, at the moment of Jesus' death — Mark 15:38 (WEB)
scriptureText: a new and living way, which he dedicated for us, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh.
weight: The breaking in your life may be the tearing of a veil. We assume that what is old and familiar is therefore safe, that the long-standing thing must be the protecting thing. But some of what hangs in our lives, for all its familiarity, has been quietly keeping us at a distance — a structure, a habit of religion, a way of relating to God that felt reverent and was really just a wall. When it tears, the first feeling is loss. Something that always hung there is suddenly in pieces. Yet ask the harder question: was it keeping you near, or keeping you out? Not every barrier that falls is a tragedy. The torn veil teaches that God will sometimes rip the old wide open precisely to grant the nearness it was blocking. What feels like the rending of something sacred can turn out to be the opening of a way you could never have reached while the old thing still hung intact between you and Him.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect is not only loss; here it is doorway. The phase asks you to read the tearing rightly — to see that when an old order ends, the rending itself may be the opening of a way. What looks like pure destruction from one side is, from God's side, access granted. The break is the door.
upheaval.inYou: The breaking in your life may be a veil tearing — the end of something that, for all its familiarity, was keeping you at a distance. The first feeling is loss. The truer question is whether the old thing held you near or held you out. What feels like the rending of the sacred can be the opening of a way you could never reach while it hung intact.
upheaval.inTheBody: When an old ecclesial structure tears, the honest question is whether a veil has just been removed. Some of the church's broken barriers were quietly keeping people out of the holy place while everyone called them reverent. The torn veil is the pattern: God will sometimes rip the old order wide open in order to grant the very access it had been blocking.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the access itself — the new and living way opened through the torn veil. Curtains and structures can be rent; the open road into God's presence cannot be closed again. When the old barriers fall, what remains is nearer than the barriers ever let you come: the way standing open.
reflection: What in my life that has torn might actually have been a veil keeping me at a distance?
Where have I mistaken a wall for something sacred simply because it was familiar?
Am I grieving a barrier God tore down to bring me nearer than it ever allowed?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, You tore the veil from the top, with Your own hand, to open the way to Yourself. When the old things in my life tear, give me eyes to see whether You are removing a wall that kept me distant. Lead me through the torn veil into the nearness I could never reach before. Amen.

notes.primary: Mark 15:38 (the veil torn top to bottom); Hebrews 10:20 (a new and living way through the veil).

title: The look that found Peter
moment: Not every disconnect is one we choose nobly. Some are the breaks of our own failing, and this is one of the hardest in the Gospels. Peter, who had sworn he never would, who had drawn a sword for his Lord only hours before, now stands in a courtyard by a charcoal fire and denies Him. Once. Twice. A third time, with cursing. And just then the cock crows, and across the courtyard the Lord turns and looks at him. Luke does not tell us it was a glare. He tells us only that He looked. In that look is everything Peter has done and everything Peter still is to Him, held together at once. And Peter remembers the word that had named this very hour, and he goes out, and he weeps bitterly. There it is — the most devastating break a person can know, the one we cause ourselves, the failure we were certain we would never commit. And the look that finds us inside it is not the end of hope. For Peter, across the dark days ahead, that look was the beginning of grace, not its closing.
voiceQuote: The Lord turned, and looked at Peter.
scriptureText: He went out, and wept bitterly.
weight: Maybe the rupture you are living was your own doing — a denial, a betrayal, a collapse you swore you would never be capable of, and then were. There is a particular agony in the breaks we cannot blame on anyone else. The self-inflicted wound carries its own voice, and the voice says: this one disqualifies you, this is where it ends. The courtyard says no. The Lord turned and looked at Peter, and the look did not finish him; it found him. The bitter weeping that follows is not the sound of a door closing. For Peter it was the doorway back — the grief that grace uses to bring a man home. Your failure is real, and naming it honestly matters; this is no airbrushing of sin. But a self-inflicted break is not the final word over your life. The same Lord who looked across that fire knows exactly what you did, and turns toward you still. That turning is where restoration begins.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect includes the breaks we cause ourselves — not the noble rupture but the shameful one. The phase asks something hard here: to let the failure be real without letting it be final, and to receive the look that finds you in it. The break of your own making is still a break God can meet, and even use.
upheaval.inYou: Maybe the rupture you are living was your own failure — a denial, a betrayal, a collapse you swore you would never commit. The Lord's look finds you there too, and it is not a glare. The bitter weeping is not the end of you; for Peter it was the doorway back. Self-inflicted breaks are real, but they are not the final word over your life.
upheaval.inTheBody: The church breaks faith with its Lord as well — denies Him in cowardice, fails in public, weeps about it only later. Peter's story is the church's own story. The look that finds the failure is not condemnation but the first step of a restoration already on its way. A community that has denied its Lord is not therefore finished with Him, nor He with it.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the Lord's turning toward you in the failure. Your faithfulness gave way; His did not. The look across the fire holds both the truth of what you did and the welcome still extended. When your own collapse has shaken everything, His unbroken grace toward you remains.
reflection: What self-inflicted break am I treating as the end of my story?
Can I believe the Lord's look finds me rather than only condemns me?
Where is bitter weeping over my own failure being made into a doorway back?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, the worst break in my life is the one I caused — I denied what I swore I would defend, and I know it. You turned and looked at Peter, and the look was grace. Turn toward me now. Let my weeping be the doorway back, and begin in me the restoration only You can. Amen.

notes.primary: Luke 22:61-62 (the Lord looked at Peter; he wept bitterly).

title: Saul on the road
moment: Saul is riding hard for Damascus, arrest warrants folded in his bag, when the light throws him to the ground. He had been the most zealous defender of the old order alive, certain to his bones that he was serving God by hunting down the followers of the Way. And out of the light comes a voice that names him and undoes him in the same word: Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me. Me. The One he thought he was defending God against is the One he has been wounding. In a single instant the whole framework he had built his life upon lies in pieces in the dust, and the man who arrived as the persecutor cannot even see; they have to lead him by the hand into the city. For three days he sits blind in the dark. Then Ananias comes, and something like scales falls from his eyes, and he can see, and he rises and is baptized. The break of conversion can be exactly this violent — a life cut cleanly in two, a before and an after with a flash of light between them, the persecutor unmade so that the apostle can be born.
voiceQuote: He fell on the earth, and heard a voice saying to him, Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?
voiceAttribution: Luke, of Saul on the Damascus road — Acts 9:4 (WEB)
scriptureText: Immediately there fell from his eyes as it were scales, and he received his sight; and he arose and was baptized.
weight: God sometimes interrupts a life mid-stride, hard enough to put a person flat on the ground in the road. We picture conversion and renewal as gentle, a slow warming, a quiet turning. Sometimes it is. But sometimes it is a light that knocks you down and takes your sight and leaves you groping in the dark for three days, no longer sure of the one thing you were surest of. If your upheaval did that to you — if it cut your life cleanly into before and after and left you blind for a stretch — you are in old and good company. Do not despair of the blindness. Saul did not arrange the scales to fall; he sat in the dark and waited, and in their own time they fell. The violence of the break is not a sign that God has abandoned you to it. For the man on the Damascus road, being struck down was the beginning of seeing, and the blindness was never meant to last.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect can come as violent conversion — not a gradual turning but a life cut cleanly in two. The phase asks you to let the old framework lie broken in the dust rather than scrambling to reassemble it, and to sit in the blindness in trust. The break that knocks you flat may be the very thing clearing your eyes.
upheaval.inYou: God sometimes interrupts a life mid-stride, hard enough to put a person flat on the ground. If your upheaval knocked you down and took your sight for a while, you are in old and good company. The scales fall in their own time; the blindness is not forever; the break that felled you was the beginning of seeing, not the end of it.
upheaval.inTheBody: The church's fiercest opponents have become its greatest apostles. No one is beyond the Damascus break, and a community should hold that stubborn hope even for those who are persecuting it now. The God who stopped Saul on the road still turns enemies into builders of the very thing they set out to destroy. The persecutor may yet be the apostle.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the Lord who meets us on the road. Frameworks shatter, certainties collapse, sight itself can be taken for a time. But the voice that named Saul holds steady through all of it. When your whole world has been cut in two, the One who stopped you on the road remains, and He is not done with you.
reflection: Where has an upheaval cut my life cleanly into a before and an after?
Am I scrambling to rebuild an old framework God has let fall to pieces in the dust?
Can I sit in the blindness and trust that the scales will fall in their own time?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, You stopped Saul on the road and undid him to remake him. If You have knocked me flat and taken my sight for a season, help me not to despair of the dark. I will wait for the scales to fall. Let the break that felled me be the beginning of seeing. Amen.

notes.primary: Acts 9:4, 18 (Saul struck down on the road; scales fall from his eyes).

title: Counted as loss
moment: Years after the road to Damascus, Paul sits down and does the arithmetic of his own life out loud. He had a ledger any devout man would envy: circumcised on the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, a Pharisee, blameless under the law, the kind of pedigree that opened every door and silenced every doubt. All of it once sat in the gain column, totaled and proud. Then he draws a line through the page. Whatever things were gain to him, he says, these he has counted loss for Christ. He does not stop there. Beside the surpassing worth of knowing Jesus, the whole impressive sum is refuse — the word is blunt, the word for garbage, for what you scrape off and throw out. Notice he is not confessing that his credentials were sins. They were real assets, hard-won and genuine. He is saying they were the wrong currency. Set next to Christ they would not even spend. So he reckons them up one last time and deliberately moves the entire balance across the page, from gain to loss, eyes open, on purpose.
voiceQuote: What things were gain to me, these have I counted loss for Christ.
scriptureText: I count all things to be loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord... and count them but refuse, that I may gain Christ.
weight: The break sometimes comes for the very things you have banked your identity on. Not your obvious failures, those are easy to disown, but your achievements, the credentials you were proudest of, the record you would hand anyone who asked who you are. An upheaval can ask you to recount all of it and write the word loss beside the line that used to read gain. This is not self-hatred, and it is not pretending the achievements never happened. It is honest re-pricing. The things you are being asked to release were real, but they were never worth what He is, and the moment you set them beside Him the difference is plain. A divided ledger keeps you wealthy and unfree, your worth scattered across a dozen assets that an upheaval can liquidate in an afternoon. The clean accounting Paul models is the freer one: count it loss, call it what it is, and quit defending a net worth that was never the point. What looks like a write-off is the beginning of true gain.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect, here, is the break made on purpose and with open eyes. It does not wait for crisis to strip you; it asks you to do the stripping yourself, to recount the old credentials and deliberately reckon them loss. The phase demands a clear-eyed re-pricing of everything you have called gain, and the courage to move the balance across the page.
upheaval.inYou: Your upheaval may ask you to recount the very things you built your identity on and to reckon them loss beside Christ. Hear it rightly: this is not contempt for what you have done. It is honest re-pricing. What He is asking you to release was real, but it was never worth what He is, and you will not miss it once you see Him clearly.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church can be rich in the wrong currency too, clinging to its prestige, its reputation, its pedigree and institutional gains as if they were the treasure. The body that can sit down and recount its assets, and name the idols among them as refuse, is free to gain Christ in a way the self-impressed church never can. The proud ledger is exactly what keeps it poor toward God.
upheaval.whatRemains: When every credential is reckoned loss, what is left in the gain column cannot be shaken: the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus. Every other asset can be liquidated by an upheaval. He cannot. He is the one possession no write-off touches and no reversal undoes.
reflection: What have I quietly banked my identity on that an upheaval could liquidate in an afternoon?
Which of my gains am I afraid to recount, because I suspect Christ would price them differently?
Am I willing to call my proudest credentials loss, not because they were sins, but because He is worth more?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have kept a proud ledger and counted as gain what was never the treasure. Teach me the honest arithmetic Paul made. Help me reckon my credentials loss beside the surpassing worth of knowing You, and to do it with open eyes, gladly, for I would gain Christ. Amen.

notes.primary: Philippians 3:7-8 (what was gain, counted loss; all things refuse to gain Christ).

title: Sent out from Antioch
moment: At Antioch the break turns corporate and outward. This is no failing church being disciplined; it is one of the healthiest congregations in the world, gifted, multiethnic, well taught, the very place where believers were first called Christians. Its leaders are worshiping and fasting when the Holy Spirit speaks into the room: set apart Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them. Read that slowly. Of all the things the Spirit might ask of a thriving church, He asks for its two best men. Barnabas, the bridge-builder, the one who first vouched for the dangerous convert. Saul, the towering teacher. The Spirit does not request the spare capacity or the surplus. He asks the church to disconnect itself from its finest leaders and launch them toward a horizon no one can see. So they fast and pray, lay hands on the two, and send them away. The verb is plain and costly. They sent them away, out of the warmth of the center, into the unknown. Mission begins, as it almost always does, with a sending that takes something real from the ones who send.
voiceQuote: As they served the Lord and fasted, the Holy Spirit said, Separate Barnabas and Saul for me, for the work to which I have called them.
voiceAttribution: Luke, of the church at Antioch — Acts 13:2 (WEB)
scriptureText: When they had fasted and prayed and laid their hands on them, they sent them away.
weight: Sometimes the break is not something done to you and not something you choose against the body; it is the body choosing, under God, to break a piece of itself off and let it go. And that hurts on both sides of the laying-on of hands. To be sent is to be pried loose from people you love and a place that formed you, set apart for a work somewhere else, and it can feel like loss to everyone in the room. It is loss. It is also obedience. The deeper temptation is the church's, not the sent one's: to keep the best where they are useful and safe, to call hoarding stewardship, to mistake a full and impressive center for health. But a body that will not release its strongest cannot multiply; it can only accumulate. The Spirit still walks into the worship of thriving churches and asks for their finest. The sending costs exactly what it looks like it costs, and the cost is the point.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect is not always a rupture forced by crisis; sometimes it is the deliberate, outward break of a healthy body sending its best away from the center. The phase asks a thriving community to loosen its grip on its own strength, to lay hands on its finest and let them go, and to feel the real cost of obedience without calling it loss alone.
upheaval.inYou: Sometimes the break is being sent, pried loose from a community you love and set apart for a work elsewhere. Do not be surprised that it aches; being sent can feel like loss to everyone involved, and it is. It is also obedience. The Spirit still says, separate this one for the work I have called him to, and the calling does not stop because it costs the leaving.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church that will not release its best people, that keeps its strength safe and useful at the center, cannot become a sending church; it can only grow heavier where it stands. Antioch models the costly outward break, laying hands on its finest and letting them go. The body that sends pieces of itself away, against its own instinct to hoard, is precisely the one that multiplies.
upheaval.whatRemains: When a church sends its best into the unknown, it can let go because the One sending them is unshakable. The center may feel thinner; the Lord of the harvest does not. What cannot be shaken is His command and His keeping, holding both the sent and the sending church when the warm familiar circle is broken open.
reflection: What strength am I holding safe at the center, calling it stewardship when it is really hoarding?
If the Spirit asked for my finest, the people or gifts I most rely on, could I lay hands on them and let go?
Have I treated being sent, or sending, as pure loss, when the cost was the very shape of obedience?
upheaval.prayer: Lord of the harvest, You ask thriving churches for their best and send them into the unknown. Loosen my grip on the strength I keep safe at the center. Make me willing to lay hands and let go, to be sent or to send, trusting the cost is not loss but obedience. Amen.

notes.primary: Acts 13:2-3 (the Spirit sets apart Barnabas and Saul; they are sent out).

title: What God has cleansed
moment: Peter's break is interior and seismic, and it begins on a rooftop at noon, hungry, while lunch is being made below. He falls into a trance and sees the sky open, a great sheet let down by its corners, and in it every kind of creature his Scriptures had taught him to refuse. A voice says, rise, kill, and eat. He recoils on reflex: never, Lord, I have never eaten anything common or unclean. And the answer overturns a lifetime in a single sentence. What God has cleansed, do not call unholy. Three times the vision comes, until the refusal itself is pried out of his hands. He is being disconnected from categories he had always assumed were not opinions but God's own boundaries, the very architecture of holy and profane. While he is still turning it over, men arrive from a Roman centurion's house, and the meaning lands. The sheet was never really about food. By the time he stands in the home of Cornelius, a Gentile, on the far side of a wall he had never once thought to question, the wall is already down, and Peter says it plainly: I truly perceive that God shows no partiality.
voiceQuote: What God has cleansed, you must not make unholy.
scriptureText: Truly I perceive that God doesn't show favoritism.
weight: The hardest break is not always the loss of something you loved. Sometimes it is the falling of a boundary you were certain God Himself had drawn. Those breaks cut deeper than grief, because they cut into certainty. You can grieve a loss and still know which way is up; but when the line you policed as sacred turns out to be a line God is erasing, the floor of your confidence tilts. Peter does not get there by argument; he gets there by a vision repeated until his reflex gives way and then by watching God pour out the same Spirit on the wrong people. The discipline this asks of you is severe and rare: to hold even your boundaries with an open hand, to keep asking whether the thing you have been confidently calling unclean is something God has already cleansed. Not every line dissolves; the LORD draws real ones. But when an upheaval runs straight to the border of your certainty, it is worth wondering who is doing the erasing.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect here is the break from old boundaries, the falling of categories you held as sacred. This is the most disorienting form of the phase, because it severs not a comfort but a certainty. It asks you to loosen your grip on the very lines you assumed were God's own, and to let Him cleanse what you have been confident to call unclean.
upheaval.inYou: God may be dismantling a boundary you have held as holy, a category of people, a rule, a line you were sure He had drawn. When the break runs right to the borders of your certainty, do not assume the certainty is God. Ask, humbly and honestly, whether the LORD is cleansing the very thing you have been calling unclean, and whether your refusal is reflex rather than faith.
upheaval.inTheBody: The church's great breaks have often been the falling of walls it assumed were divine, the Gentile question first, and walls since that God tore down ahead of His reluctant people. A community must hold even its boundaries humbly. The LORD reserves the right to cleanse what we have called unholy, and the body that polices its lines as His own keeps finding Him on the other side.
upheaval.whatRemains: When the boundaries you trusted come down, the God behind them does not. His impartial mercy was the deeper truth the wall obscured. What cannot be shaken is His own holiness and His freedom to cleanse, the LORD who shows no partiality, standing firm precisely where our certainties give way.
reflection: What boundary have I policed as sacred that God may be quietly erasing?
Is my refusal of someone or something faith, or only reflex dressed as conviction?
Where might God already be standing on the other side of a wall I assumed was His?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have called some lines Your own that were only mine, and policed them as if You needed defending. Where You are cleansing what I have called unclean, soften my reflex and open my hand. Teach me to follow You past the walls You are tearing down. Amen.

notes.primary: Acts 10:15, 34 (what God has cleansed; God shows no partiality).

title: Scattered, and preaching
moment: Not every disconnect is chosen; some are inflicted from outside, by people who mean only to destroy. On the day Stephen is buried, a great persecution erupts against the church in Jerusalem, and a young man named Saul goes house to house, dragging out men and women. The community that had been so visibly one, breaking bread together and holding everything in common, is broken apart and driven from the city, scattered through the regions of Judea and Samaria, all of them except the apostles. Read it as the persecutors did and it is a victory: the troublesome sect dispersed, its center emptied, its people running for their lives. It looks like pure catastrophe, the church shattered and homeless. And then comes the line that turns the whole scene inside out. Those who were scattered abroad went around preaching the word. The very dispersion meant to extinguish the gospel carried it everywhere, like seed flung off a threshing floor by a wind that thought it was scattering chaff. What broke the church apart is precisely what planted it across the world. The catastrophe was the sowing.
