The pilgrim accepts not belonging here, not because he loves exile, but because the homeland he is seeking lies elsewhere, and he has seen it from far enough off to leave everything else behind. You are not lost. You are on the road that all of them walked, looking for a country of your own.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect, at its most uprooting. The phase here asks whether you will leave not only what is wrong but what is dear and familiar, the whole comfortable world, for the sake of an obedience that makes you a stranger. It asks you to hold the homelessness honestly and to keep walking toward a homeland you have only seen from far off.
upheaval.inYou: Some breaks ask you to pull up every root and become a stranger somewhere new for the sake of following God. If your obedience has left you not belonging here, you have not wandered off the path. You are walking in the oldest company of faith, the pilgrims who accept being aliens in this land because the homeland they seek is elsewhere.
upheaval.inTheBody: The church is at its truest a pilgrim people, never fully at home in any land or age, ready to cross an ocean rather than betray conscience. A community that has grown too comfortably native to its culture has quietly forgotten its own confession, that it is a company of strangers on the earth, still seeking a country of its own.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the homeland itself. Lands and houses and the belonging they offer can all be left behind, and one day removed entirely. But the country the pilgrim seeks is the one that remains when everything shakable is gone, and the God who promised it does not move.
reflection: What roots is God asking me to pull up, and am I treating the cost as a wrong turn or as obedience?
Where have I grown so at home in my surroundings that I have forgotten I am a stranger on the earth?
What homeland am I actually living toward, and have I seen it clearly enough to leave lesser things behind?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, You have made me a stranger here, and some days the homelessness is heavy. Give me the pilgrim's heart that can let go of what is dear for the sake of obeying You. Keep my eyes on the homeland I have seen from far off, the country that cannot be shaken. Amen.

notes.primary: Hebrews 11:13-14 (strangers and pilgrims, seeking a homeland); Hebrews 11:9 (dwelling as an alien in tents).
notes.tradition: References the English Separatists / Pilgrims who sailed to the New World (1620) for freedom to worship; public domain history, paraphrased.

title: A heart strangely warmed
moment: By every outward measure John Wesley had arrived. He was an ordained priest of the Church of England, an Oxford man, the leader of a disciplined religious society, a missionary who had crossed the Atlantic and come home again. And by his own account he was cold. He had striven and failed, kept the rules and felt nothing, carried all the apparatus of faith with none of its fire. Then came an evening in 1738 that asked nothing of him but to sit and listen. At a meeting on Aldersgate Street someone was reading aloud Luther's preface to the letter to the Romans, and as the words moved through the room something gave way in the religious professional who had thought he had no further to go. He felt, as he later put it, his heart strangely warmed. For the first time he trusted Christ alone to save him, and knew the saving was done. The break, it turns out, can come even to the man who runs the meeting. The disconnect Wesley needed was not from heresy or scandal but from dead duty into living faith, the move from religion kept to a clean heart received. He had been creating nothing in himself; now it was created in him.
voiceQuote: Create in me a clean heart, God; renew a right spirit within me.
scriptureText: Not by works of righteousness which we did ourselves, but according to his mercy, he saved us, through the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit.
weight: You can be inside the faith for years and still need this break. You can serve, lead, teach, give, do everything right, and remain a stranger to the living thing underneath it all, running on duty and willpower and the quiet exhaustion of a heart that has never been warmed. If that is you, Wesley is good news, because he shows that it is never too late and no role too senior for the break from religion-as-performance into living trust. The most accomplished insider in the room can still be the one who most needs to be broken open. And notice the shape of it: the clean heart is not a wage you finally earn by enough effort. It is a gift you receive, often in the moment you stop striving and simply let the truth be read over you. If your faith has gone cold while your duties stayed warm, the answer is not to try harder at the performance. It is to let God create in you the thing you cannot manufacture, and to trust Christ alone for it.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect, turned inward. This is the break from dead religion into living faith, and the phase insists it can come even to the lifelong professional, the one who keeps every rule and feels nothing. It asks you to stop running on duty and willpower and to let the heart itself be broken open and warmed.
upheaval.inYou: You can be inside the faith for years, serving and leading and doing everything right, and still need the break from religion-as-performance into living trust. Wesley shows it is never too late, and no role too senior, for the heart to be strangely warmed. The clean heart is a gift to receive in the moment you stop striving, not a wage you earn.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church full of competent religion can still be cold, and its deepest renewals often begin when the professionals themselves are broken open into living faith. A whole revival traced back to one warmed heart in a quiet meeting. God has a habit of renewing the body by first renewing its weary, dutiful insiders, the very people sure they had no further to go.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the work that saves you, which was never yours to perform. Your cold seasons and your fervent ones rise and fall like weather. But Christ's finished mercy, the washing of regeneration you can only receive, holds steady beneath the changing temperature of your heart, and it does not depend on the strength of your striving.
reflection: Where am I running on duty and willpower, doing everything right while my heart stays cold?
Have I been trying to earn a clean heart as a wage rather than receiving it as a gift?
Do I secretly believe my role or experience puts me past the need for this kind of break?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have kept the rules and felt nothing, carrying the shape of faith without its fire. I cannot warm my own heart. Create in me a clean heart and renew a right spirit within me. Let me stop striving and simply trust Christ alone to save me, today. Amen.

notes.primary: Psalm 51:10 (create in me a clean heart); Titus 3:5 (saved by the washing of regeneration).
notes.tradition: References John Wesley's Aldersgate experience (1738), when his heart was strangely warmed; public domain, paraphrased.

title: Revive your work
moment: By the 1730s the churches of the American colonies had settled into a comfortable chill. The forms were intact, the pews filled on Sundays, the doctrine sound enough, and the life had quietly drained out of it all. Religion had become a thing inherited and managed rather than felt. Then something broke in that no one had scheduled. Under the searching preaching of Jonathan Edwards, who could hold a congregation over the edge of eternity until it trembled, and the open-air voice of George Whitefield, who preached to thousands in fields no church wall could hold, a great awakening swept across the land. People who had been nominally Christian their whole lives were jolted into something vivid and undone, weeping over sin they had never taken seriously, their settled lives reordered in a season. It looked less like a program than a flood. This is a kind of break the phase has to name, because it does not come by leaving. It comes by waking. Revival is a corporate disconnect, God breaking a sleeping church out of its own deadness, against the grain of its settled inertia. No committee voted for it. It arrived like weather, and the dry, formal religion it found could not stand in front of it.
voiceQuote: The LORD, I have heard of your fame; I stand in awe of your deeds. Renew your work in the midst of the years; in wrath, you remember mercy.
scriptureText: Won't you revive us again, that your people may rejoice in you?
weight: Sometimes the break you need is not to leave but to wake. You have not walked away from the faith; you have simply gone numb inside it, your love grown nominal, your prayers gone formal, the whole thing running on memory and habit. That sleep is its own kind of captivity, and you usually cannot shake yourself out of it by trying. Revival is God's disruptive mercy for exactly this, the in-breaking that jolts a cold heart awake against its own inertia. It is not always gentle, and it is rarely convenient, but it is mercy. And here is what you can do with a numb and sleepy faith: you can ask for the disruption. You can pray the prophet's prayer over your own cold heart, that God would renew His work in the midst of your years, that He would revive you again. You cannot manufacture the fire. But you can stop defending the sleep and start asking to be woken, which is the one move a slumbering heart is still free to make.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect, as awakening. Not every break is a leaving; this one is God breaking a sleeping church and a sleeping heart out of settled deadness, against their own inertia. The phase asks whether you will defend your numbness or ask to be woken, and whether you will let a disruption you cannot control reorder a faith gone formal.
upheaval.inYou: Sometimes the break you need is not to leave but to wake, to be jolted out of a faith gone nominal and sleepy into something alive again. Revival is God's disruptive mercy, and the one move a numb heart is still free to make is to ask for it. Pray the prophet's prayer over your own coldness: renew Your work, Lord, in the midst of my years.
upheaval.inTheBody: Churches calcify, and God has a long habit of breaking in with revival, awakening a sleeping body, often through unlikely preachers and against the establishment's comfort. A community can ask for this disruption, can pray to be revived again. The awakening is a break from deadness no church can manufacture or schedule, only seek and then make room for when it comes.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the God who revives. Fervor rises and cools, awakenings pass into memory, the warmest church can drift back toward sleep. But the One who breaks in to wake the dead is unchanged from age to age, and the work He renews in the midst of the years is His to keep alive, not ours.
reflection: Where has my faith gone numb and formal, running on habit and memory rather than life?
Am I defending my spiritual sleep, or am I willing to ask God to disrupt it?
What would it mean to pray honestly, renew Your work in the midst of my years, and then make room for the answer?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have gone cold inside a faith I never left, and I cannot wake myself. Break in with Your disruptive mercy. Renew Your work in the midst of my years, and revive me again, that I might rejoice in You. I stop defending the sleep and ask to be woken. Amen.

notes.primary: Habakkuk 3:2 (renew your work in the midst of the years); Psalm 85:6 (revive us again).
notes.tradition: References the Great Awakening (c. 1730s-40s), Jonathan Edwards and George Whitefield; public domain history, paraphrased.

title: Enlarge the tent
moment: He was a shoemaker who taught himself languages over his last, a country preacher of no great standing, and he had become convinced of something the church around him had quietly stopped believing: that the command to make disciples of all nations still stood, and the unreached peoples were waiting to hear. When the young William Carey pressed this on a gathering of ministers in 1792, an elder, by the account handed down, told him to sit down: if God meant to convert the heathen, He would do it without the likes of Carey. It was complacency speaking in the accent of piety, smallness calling itself trust in providence. Carey would not sit down. He pressed the church to expect great things from God and to attempt great things for God, and where others heard the limits of prudence he heard a tent whose cords had been left too short: enlarge the place of your tent, Isaiah had said, lengthen the cords, strengthen the stakes. So he founded a society and sailed for India, into a labor that would consume his life. His refusal to sit down shattered a complacency that had let the church forget the nations, and out of that one break the modern missionary movement was born.
voiceQuote: Enlarge the place of your tent... lengthen your cords, and strengthen your stakes.
scriptureText: How will they call on him in whom they have not believed? How will they believe in him whom they have not heard? And how will they hear without a preacher?
weight: Sometimes the break is simply being unwilling to sit down. Everyone around you has quietly accepted a smallness, a settled boundary on what God might do, a polite limit dressed up as wisdom and prudence and providence, and the upheaval God asks of you is to refuse it. That refusal will feel presumptuous, because complacency always sounds reasonable and the person who questions it always sounds like they are overreaching. Carey's disconnect was from exactly this: a comfortable smallness that everyone called prudence, a boundary no one had thought to question in years. And here is the cost the image of the tent makes plain. Enlarging it always means breaking the comfortable line of the stakes right where they are. You cannot lengthen the cords without pulling up the pegs that felt so settled and driving them out into ground that frightens you. If God is stirring you to attempt something larger than the room around you thinks reasonable, the break may be a holy one, the refusal to keep sitting down when grace is calling you to stand.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect, breaking outward. The phase here is not a turning inward but a refusal to keep the good news small, a break from a complacency that had decided the world need not be reached. It asks whether you will sit down with everyone else or pull up the comfortable stakes and let the tent be enlarged into ground that frightens you.
upheaval.inYou: Sometimes the break is being unwilling to sit down, refusing a complacency everyone around you has quietly accepted. Carey's disconnect was from a settled smallness that called itself prudence. If God is stirring you toward something larger than the room thinks reasonable, remember that enlarging the tent always means breaking the comfortable boundary of the stakes right where they are.
upheaval.inTheBody: Churches grow inward and forget the nations, dressing complacency as theology. God breaks that inertia through people who will not sit down, who insist the cords be lengthened and the stakes driven wider. The missionary break is the church refusing to keep the good news to itself, and a body that never produces such people has settled for a tent too small.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the reach of the gospel itself. Complacencies harden and are broken, boundaries are drawn and driven wider, but the command to carry the good news to all nations does not contract to fit a church's comfort. The mission stands when our settled smallness is shaken away, resting on the unchanging will of God.
reflection: What settled smallness around me have I quietly accepted as prudence rather than questioned as complacency?
Where is God stirring me to attempt something larger than the people around me think reasonable?
Which comfortable stakes is He asking me to pull up so the tent can be enlarged?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have grown comfortable inside boundaries I never questioned and called my smallness wisdom. Give me the holy refusal to sit down when You are calling me to stand. Help me expect great things from You and attempt great things for You, and to let the stakes be driven wider, wherever that leads. Amen.

notes.primary: Isaiah 54:2 (enlarge your tent); Romans 10:14 (how will they hear without a preacher?).
notes.tradition: References William Carey (1792), the modern missionary movement, and his call to expect and attempt great things for God; public domain, paraphrased.

title: Open your mouth
moment: In 1934 the official German church was bending to the Nazi state, remaking the gospel to fit a regime. To many it looked like loyalty. To a group of Christians who could not stomach it, it looked like a church selling its soul. They broke away to form what was called the Confessing Church, and at Barmen they set their refusal down in writing: the church has one Lord, Jesus Christ, and owes no rival allegiance to any earthly ruler or ideology. It was a line drawn through the heart of a captured institution. Among those who stood on the far side of it was a young pastor, Dietrich Bonhoeffer, who would give his short life to the resistance and pay for the break with his death. Mark what the disconnect was and was not. It was not a break over a fine point of doctrine. It was a break from a church that had fused itself to worldly power and called the fusion devotion, a refusal to be silent while the desolate were crushed. The mother of King Lemuel had charged her son to open his mouth for the mute, in the cause of all left desolate. At Barmen a remnant remembered that charge when the rest forgot it.
voiceQuote: Open your mouth for the mute, in the cause of all who are left desolate.
voiceAttribution: The mother of King Lemuel — Proverbs 31:8 (WEB)
scriptureText: To him who knows to do good, and doesn't do it, to him it is sin.
weight: There are breaks that conscience demands when the institution you belong to begins going along with evil. They are the costliest of all, because the pressure to stay is dressed as loyalty, and the people leaning on you to keep quiet are often the ones you most want to please. To open your mouth for those who cannot speak, to separate yourself from a comfortable complicity, can cost you your standing, your security, and, as it cost some at Barmen, your life. This is not a break to romanticize from a safe distance. It is meant to sober you. The temptation in such a moment is to tell yourself that silence is prudence, that staying inside lets you do more good, that the time to speak has not quite come. James cuts through all of it: to the one who knows to do good and does not do it, that failure is itself sin. Sometimes the only faithful move is the costly break, and the refusal to make it is not neutrality. It is the sin of knowing the good and declining to do it.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect, at its most costly. This is the break of conscience from a church co-opted by worldly power, the separation that may cost everything. The phase asks whether you will name complicity as complicity rather than loyalty, and whether you will open your mouth for the desolate even when silence is safer and the cost of speaking is real.
upheaval.inYou: There are breaks demanded by conscience when the institution you belong to goes along with evil. To open your mouth for those who cannot speak, to break from a comfortable complicity, can cost you everything. And silence is not the neutral safe ground it pretends to be. Knowing the good and refusing to do it, James says bluntly, is itself sin.
upheaval.inTheBody: The church is perpetually tempted to fuse with worldly power and call it loyalty. Sometimes faithfulness requires a costly break from a co-opted church, as at Barmen, where a remnant declared that Christ alone is Lord. A body that will not, when the moment comes, separate itself from complicity with evil has already lost the only Lord it claims to serve.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the church's one true Lord. Institutions bend to power and are exposed; allegiances that called themselves loyalty are torn away. But the lordship of Jesus Christ over His church does not yield to any earthly ruler or ideology, and it stands unmoved when every counterfeit devotion is shaken to the ground.
reflection: Where is an institution I belong to going along with something I know to be wrong?
Am I calling my silence prudence when conscience knows it is complicity?
Whom is God asking me to open my mouth for, even if speaking costs me dearly?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, when those around me fuse faith to power and call it loyalty, give me eyes to see it and courage to refuse it. Help me open my mouth for those who cannot speak, whatever it costs. Keep me from the sin of knowing the good and staying silent. You alone are Lord. Amen.

notes.primary: Proverbs 31:8 (open your mouth for the mute); James 4:17 (knowing the good and not doing it).
notes.tradition: References Dietrich Bonhoeffer and the Confessing Church's break from the Nazified German state church (the Barmen Declaration, 1934). Bonhoeffer's own writings are under copyright and are not quoted — only his actions and the historical events are referenced.

title: New things I declare
moment: We are living, by many accounts, inside one of the great upheavals that come round roughly every five hundred years. Phyllis Tickle named our version of it the Great Emergence, and likened the church to a house that periodically holds a giant rummage sale, clearing the attic of what no longer serves so the rooms can breathe again. From inside, it does not feel like housecleaning. It feels like the floor moving. The certainties of Christendom are cracking. Institutions that stood for generations are wobbling. A whole generation is laying its inherited faith out on the lawn, sorting, questioning, asking out loud where the authority finally lies. If you have felt the ground shift under the church you were raised in, you are not imagining it, and you are not alone in it. But the pattern is older than your fear. God has poured out His Spirit in such breaks before, on sons and daughters who thought the old world was ending. He is the kind of God who tells you of the new thing before it springs forth, while the former things are still falling. The shaking is loud. It is not, by itself, the end.
voiceQuote: It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy.
scriptureText: Behold, the former things have happened, and new things do I declare; before they spring forth I tell you of them.
weight: It changes things to know you were born into a hinge. Your private upheaval is real, and this does not shrink it, but it does set it inside something far larger than your own story. The doubts you carry, the church that disappointed you, the certainties that came apart in your hands, the sense that the whole edifice is groaning at once, you did not invent any of it alone in a room. You were handed a season. Whole eras of believers before you have stood exactly here, watching the old shell crack, terrified it meant the faith itself was failing. It did not. Every time, the cracking was the front edge of a renewal nobody in the rubble could yet see. That is not a promise that the institution you grew up in survives unchanged. Most of them did not. It is a promise about the One doing the shaking. Ask the steadying question underneath the panic: is what is falling the faith itself, or only the latest house the faith was living in? He declares new things before they spring forth. You are early in one of them.

upheaval.thePhase: This is Disconnect on the scale of an age. The phase asks you to stop reading the shaking of the church as its death certificate, and to recognize it instead as the painful opening of a renewal you cannot yet see. Disconnect, here, means trusting the pattern when the institutions crack: God has done this before.
upheaval.inYou: The break you are living is not only yours. You were set down inside a moment when the whole church is being shaken at once, and that is unsettling, but it means your small upheaval is folded into something vast that God is doing. The former things are passing. You are not watching the end. You are standing at a beginning.
upheaval.inTheBody: Roughly every five centuries the church holds its rummage sale, and the evidence says we are inside one. Institutions wobble, inherited certainties crack, and it feels like collapse. But the body has been here before, and the shaking was never the end of the faith, only the front edge of its next renewal. God has poured out His Spirit in such breaks, and says He is doing it again.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is not the house but the Lord of the house. Christendom is a structure, and structures get cleared out; the kingdom He is building cannot be removed. Hebrews says as much: the shaking comes precisely so that what cannot be shaken may remain.
reflection: Have I been mistaking the shaking of the church I knew for the failing of the faith itself?
What in my inherited Christianity is being laid out on the lawn right now, and can I trust the One sorting it?
If I was born into a hinge of history, how does that change the way I carry my own upheaval?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, the whole house seems to be moving, and I am frightened by how much is falling. Remind me You have done this before, and poured out Your Spirit in the breaking. Show me what is only the old shell cracking, and hold me steady while You declare the new thing. Amen.

notes.primary: Joel 2:28 (I will pour out my Spirit); Isaiah 42:9 (new things I declare).
notes.tradition: References the present cultural-ecclesial upheaval that Phyllis Tickle called the Great Emergence (The Great Emergence, 2008), arriving roughly five centuries after the Reformation; paraphrased and attributed.

title: Born anew
moment: Beneath every great break in these pages lies the one break every Christian shares. A respectable man comes to Jesus at night, careful, credentialed, a teacher of Israel who wants to talk theology in the dark. And Jesus will not let him stay on that ground. Unless one is born anew, He says, he cannot even see the Kingdom of God. Not improved. Not reformed. Not coached into a better version of the same life. Born again, from the very beginning, as if from nothing. Nicodemus balks at the picture, because birth is precisely the wrong metaphor for self-improvement. You cannot ease your way into being born. It is total and it is involuntary; one mode of existence ends and another begins, and there is no gentle gradient between them. That is the scandal Jesus presses on a man who had done everything right. To come to Christ is not to add faith to a life otherwise intact. It is a disconnect from the old self so complete that Scripture can find no smaller word for it than new birth, a death and a beginning in the same breath.
voiceQuote: Unless one is born anew, he can't see the Kingdom of God.
scriptureText: Having been born again, not of corruptible seed, but of incorruptible, through the word of God, which lives and remains forever.
weight: Your first and deepest break was meant to be this one. Before any church split, any leaving, any crisis that cracked the ground, there was supposed to be a morning you passed from death to life and did not stay the person you had been. If that feels long ago and faint now, worn smooth by years of ordinary Tuesdays, it is worth remembering what it actually was. Not a mild adjustment to your worldview. Not a decision you filed away. A rupture. The old self does not negotiate its own death, which is why Jesus speaks of being born from above, something done to you and for you, not something you arranged. And here is the quiet mercy in it: the seed planted in that birth was incorruptible. It does not rot. The new life it began is not a phase you can age out of or a flame you can finally let gutter. You may have wandered far from the warmth of it. The seed is still alive. The One who began that work in you was never depending on your memory of the day to keep it going.

upheaval.thePhase: This is Disconnect at its root, the break beneath all the others. The phase asks you to recognize conversion not as a tame turning-over of a new leaf but as the death of an old self and the birth of a new one. Before you can leave anything else, this is the leaving that made you a Christian at all.
upheaval.inYou: Your deepest break was meant to be conversion, the end of the old self and the start of a wholly new life in Christ. If that birth feels distant and dim now, do not downgrade what it was. It was a real rupture, not a soft adjustment. And the seed sown in it is incorruptible; the life it began does not die.
upheaval.inTheBody: The church is a community of the born-again, not the merely improved, each one having passed through the break of new birth. When a church forgets this, when it offers faith as a gentle enhancement to a life left otherwise intact rather than a death and a resurrection, it has misplaced the very disconnect that made it the church.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the incorruptible seed itself, the new life God began and guarantees. Feelings fade and the memory of the day grows faint, but the birth was His doing and His to keep. Hebrews speaks of a kingdom that cannot be shaken; this new life belongs to it.
reflection: Do I treat my conversion as a real death and birth, or as a mild improvement I once made?
If the warmth of that day has gone faint, what would it mean to trust the seed is still alive?
Where have I been trying to improve the old self that Christ meant to put to death?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, You said I must be born anew, not merely made better, and I confess I often live as if a little improvement would do. Thank You that the seed You planted is incorruptible and the life You began does not die. Keep alive in me the new birth that was always Your work. Amen.

notes.primary: John 3:3 (born anew to see the Kingdom); 1 Peter 1:23 (born again of incorruptible seed).

title: They wept and embraced him
moment: Some of the most painful breaks are not from anything wrong but from something good. Paul has finished his work in Asia and called the elders of Ephesus down to the shore at Miletus to say goodbye, and he tells them plainly they will not see his face again. Then he kneels in the sand and prays with all of them, and the scene breaks open. They weep, openly, grown men falling on his neck and kissing him, grieving most of all that one word: never again. Paul does not manage their grief or hurry it along or correct it into something more composed. He does not tell them it is fine. He weeps too. And then, into the middle of that weeping, he does the only thing that makes such a parting bearable. He entrusts them, hands them over, to God and to the word of His grace, which is able to build them up far past anything his staying could have done. And he goes. The leaving is right. The grief is real. Acts lets both stand together on that beach, unresolved, a true parting between people who loved each other and a release into the keeping of God.
voiceQuote: They all wept, and fell on Paul's neck and kissed him.
scriptureText: I entrust you to God, and to the word of his grace, which is able to build up, and to give you the inheritance among all those who are sanctified.
weight: Leaving a church you have loved, a team you gave years to, a community that knew your name, can break your heart even when leaving is exactly the right thing. We are oddly unprepared for that. We assume that if a decision is correct it should not hurt, and so when the grief comes we suspect we have made a mistake, or we let someone tell us our sorrow is a sign of weak faith. It is neither. Paul wept on that shore, and no one has ever called him faithless for it. Do not let anyone, including the voice in your own head, shame the grief out of you. But do not let the grief become the whole story either. The way through is the way Paul walked: you entrust the people you are leaving to God, who can keep them and build them up far better than your staying ever could, and then you actually go. Both halves matter. The tears honor what was real. The entrusting frees you to obey. A good leaving is not a tearless one. It is a grieving one that still, in the end, lets go.

upheaval.thePhase: This is Disconnect as grief, the break from something good. The phase asks you to hold two things at once that feel like they should cancel: that a parting can be both genuinely right and genuinely heartbreaking. Disconnect here does not deny the loss; it grieves it honestly and entrusts what is left behind to God.
upheaval.inYou: Leaving a church, a team, a community you have loved can break your heart even when it is the right thing to do. Do not let anyone shame the grief; Paul wept too. The way through is his way: entrust the people you are leaving to God, who can keep and build them far better than your staying ever could.
upheaval.inTheBody: Healthy communities release people with tears rather than bitterness, grieving the loss and blessing the going at once. When someone must leave, the body's calling is to weep for them, to entrust them to God and the word of His grace, and to let them go in love rather than in guilt or grudge. A good farewell looks like that beach at Miletus.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the word of His grace, which goes on building people up long after you have left them, and the God to whom you entrust them. People are parted; the keeping is not. Hebrews promises a kingdom that cannot be shaken, and those you release in love remain held within it.
reflection: Have I let myself grieve a good leaving, or have I shamed the sorrow as a lack of faith?
Whom have I left, or must I leave, that I have not yet entrusted to God?
Am I willing to both weep honestly and actually let go, the way Paul did on the shore?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, leaving what I loved has broken my heart, and I have wondered if the grief means I got it wrong. Paul wept too, and still he went. Let me grieve honestly without shame, and then entrust the people I am leaving to You, who keep them far better than I could. Amen.

notes.primary: Acts 20:37 (the Ephesian elders weep at Paul's farewell); Acts 20:32 (I entrust you to God).

title: Help my unbelief
moment: Sometimes the break is not a leaving you decide on but a faith that simply cracks. The certainties you were handed stop bearing weight. Questions you cannot un-ask rise up and will not lie back down. The answers that satisfied you at twenty do not reach the thing that is happening to you now, and you find, to your alarm, that you are no longer sure of what you were once sure of in your bones. In the gospel a father stands in front of Jesus in exactly this condition. His son is afflicted, his hope is nearly gone, and when Jesus presses him on belief, he does not produce a confident creed. He blurts the most honest prayer in all of Scripture: I believe; help my unbelief. Both halves in one breath. Faith and the failure of faith, refusing to be separated. It is the language of a man whose old certainty has cracked clean down the middle. And here is the thing to notice, the thing that changes everything. Jesus does not wait for him to resolve the contradiction. He does not demand the doubt be cleared up first. He honors the divided cry exactly as it is, and He acts on it.
voiceQuote: I believe; help my unbelief.
voiceAttribution: The father of the afflicted boy — Mark 9:24 (WEB)
scriptureText: As for me, my feet were almost gone; my steps had nearly slipped.
weight: If your faith is cracking and the most you can manage on a given morning is I believe, help my unbelief, hear this clearly: you have not fallen out of God's reach. That broken, self-contradicting prayer is not the evidence that you are losing Him. It is enough for Jesus to act on, and He did. We have been taught, somewhere along the way, that doubt is the opposite of faith, its enemy, a thing to be ashamed of and hidden. But the opposite of faith is not honest doubt; it is indifference, the heart that has stopped caring enough to ask. The father in the story was not indifferent. He was desperate, and desperation that still turns toward Christ, however unsure, is a kind of faith. The slipping of your feet is not the end of you. The psalmist confessed that his feet had almost gone, his steps had nearly slipped, and the God he nearly stopped trusting held him anyway. This is the edge where the old certainty fails and the wilderness begins. It is frightening ground. But it is not God-forsaken ground, and the honest cry is welcome on it.

upheaval.thePhase: This is Disconnect as honest doubt, the on-ramp to the wilderness. The phase names the moment the old certainty cracks and the questions break through, and it asks you not to despise that breaking. Disconnect here is the doorway: where the inherited certainty fails, the longer journey toward a tested faith begins.
upheaval.inYou: If your faith is cracking and you can manage only I believe, help my unbelief, you have not slipped out of God's reach. That broken prayer is enough for Jesus to act on. The slipping of your feet is not the end; the psalmist nearly fell too, and God held him. Honest doubt is not the opposite of faith.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church should make room for honest doubt instead of punishing it, because the break of questioning is so often the doorway into a deeper, tested faith. A community that demands tidy certainty drives its doubters out the back; one that can hold the cry help my unbelief keeps them through the wilderness toward firmer ground.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the hand that held a man whose feet had nearly slipped, the Christ who acts on a divided cry. Your certainty can crack and your footing give way; His grip does not. Hebrews speaks of a kingdom that cannot be shaken, and the doubter who still turns toward Him is held inside it.
reflection: Have I believed the lie that my doubt has put me beyond God's reach?
Can I bring Him the honest, divided prayer instead of waiting until I feel certain again?
Where have I treated questioning as the enemy of faith rather than a doorway through it?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, my certainties have cracked, and some mornings all I can pray is that I believe and need help with my unbelief. Thank You that You honored that very cry and acted on it. Hold my feet when they slip, and lead me through the doubt toward a tested, steadier faith. Amen.

notes.primary: Mark 9:24 (I believe; help my unbelief); Psalm 73:2 (my feet had nearly slipped).

title: Call me Mara
moment: Naomi comes home to Bethlehem a hollowed woman. She had left in a famine with a husband and two sons, a whole future folded around her, and she returns with none of them, all three dead in the foreign country of Moab, her life simply emptied out. The town stirs at the sight of her, the women asking, is this Naomi? And she will not take back her own name. Naomi means pleasant, and she has nothing pleasant left to answer to. Do not call me Naomi, she says; call me Mara, bitter, for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me. Then she puts it as plainly as grief can be put: I went out full, and the LORD has brought me home again empty. There is no theology of silver linings in her mouth, no rushing toward the lesson. Some breaks are pure loss, not chosen, not noble, nothing to be admired in them, just the tearing away of what you loved most. And what is striking is that Scripture does not correct her. It lets her stand in the gate of Bethlehem and name her bitterness, to the face of the very God she holds responsible, and it does not flinch or scold.
voiceQuote: Don't call me Naomi, call me Mara; for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me.
scriptureText: I went out full, and the LORD has brought me home again empty.
weight: If your break is grief, a death, a diagnosis, a marriage gone, a life emptied of the thing you treasured, then Naomi's honesty is yours to use. You are not required to pretend the loss is secretly sweet, or to find the silver lining by Sunday, or to narrate your suffering into a tidy lesson for anyone's comfort, least of all your own. You are allowed to say, full I went out and empty I have come back. The witness of her story is that she speaks like this to God, not behind His back but to His face, and the relationship survives it. Bitterness named honestly before God is not the same as unbelief; the book of Ruth puts it right there in the canon and does not apologize for it. And here is what Naomi cannot see from inside her emptiness, what you may not see from inside yours: the same God she accuses of emptying her hand is, in that very chapter, walking home beside her in a Moabite daughter-in-law named Ruth, already quietly writing redemption into the empty place. The naming of the bitterness was never the end of her story. It was simply allowed.

upheaval.thePhase: This is Disconnect as sheer loss, the break you never chose. The phase does not demand you spin your grief into something noble; it gives you Naomi's permission to name the bitterness honestly before God. Disconnect here asks for truth-telling, not bravery, and trusts that God can be at work in an emptiness you cannot yet read.
upheaval.inYou: If your break is grief, a death, a diagnosis, a life emptied of what you treasured, you are allowed Naomi's honesty. You need not pretend the loss is sweet or hurry yourself to a lesson. Name the bitterness to God. The same God she accused of emptying her was, unseen, already writing redemption through Ruth.
upheaval.inTheBody: A community must make room for lament, for the Mara seasons when its people come home empty. A church that demands relentless positivity abandons its grieving to suffer alone. The honest naming of bitterness before God is not faithlessness; it stands in Scripture, and the God who receives it is quietly at work in the very emptiness.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the God who lets you name the bitterness and stays, already at work in the emptiness before you can see it. Lives are emptied; His redeeming purpose is not. Hebrews promises a kingdom that cannot be shaken, and even the hollowed-out are being carried toward it.
reflection: Have I given myself permission to name my loss honestly to God, or have I forced a brave face?
Where am I rushing toward a lesson when what I need is simply to lament?
Can I trust that God may be writing redemption into an emptiness I cannot yet read?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I went out full and have come home empty, and like Naomi I will not pretend the loss is sweet. Thank You that You let her say so to Your face and stayed. Receive my honest bitterness, and work, unseen, in the emptiness I cannot read, as You did through Ruth. Amen.

notes.primary: Ruth 1:20-21 (call me Mara; I went out full and came home empty).

title: Running from God
moment: Not every break runs toward God. Some are a flat sprint the other way. The word of the LORD comes to Jonah plainly enough — go to Nineveh, that great and hated city, and cry against it. Jonah hears it, stands up, and runs. He goes down to Joppa, finds a ship bound for Tarshish, the far western edge of the known world, pays the fare out of his own pocket, and climbs down into the hold to get as far from the presence of the LORD as a man can buy his way. Every verb in the scene goes downward — down to Joppa, down into the ship, down below the deck, and soon down into the deep. This is a disconnect of plain disobedience, a break a man chooses against God rather than for Him. And still the LORD will not let the running be the last word. He hurls a great wind onto the sea. He appoints a great fish. And in the wet dark of its belly, at the bottom of everything Jonah's flight has cost him, the runaway finally prays, and the prayer ends where every true return begins: salvation belongs to the LORD, and not to his own frantic escaping.
voiceQuote: Jonah rose up to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the LORD... and went down into the ship to go with them, from the presence of the LORD.
scriptureText: I will sacrifice to you with the voice of thanksgiving... salvation belongs to the LORD.
weight: Maybe your break was a running away. Not a leaving God called you to, but a deliberate flight from something He asked and you would not do — a call refused, a conviction outrun, a known good you sprinted away from and paid the fare to escape. It is worth being honest that such breaks exist, and that some of ours are them. The mercy in Jonah is that the running is not the end of the story God is telling. He pursues the disobedient disconnect. He appoints the storm that stops the flight and the fish that swallows the consequence, and He is there in the belly of it, listening, when the prayer finally comes. You cannot out-sail Him; the deep itself is His. And the way back is not a long climb of penance. It is the short, drenched confession Jonah finally gasps: that salvation is the LORD's to give, never yours to flee, and never yours to earn back by running harder in the other direction.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect names even the break we cause by running from God. This phase does not pretend every rupture is noble; some are flat disobedience. What it asks is that you stop sprinting long enough to be caught — to let the storm halt the flight and the dark teach the prayer that salvation is the LORD's.
upheaval.inYou: If your break was a running away, hear this: God pursues even that. He can redeem the disobedient disconnect, and He meets the runaway in the belly of the consequences, not only on the far shore. Your return need not be impressive. It begins the moment you stop and admit that salvation belongs to Him, not to your escaping.
upheaval.inTheBody: Churches flee callings too, sailing the other way and naming the cowardice prudence. A body can spend years and money getting downward and away from what God plainly asked. Yet the LORD has ways of bringing a runaway people to the end of themselves, into a dark and narrow place where, at last, they pray. The disobedient break is not past His reach.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the LORD's hold on the one who fled. Your flight can be removed, the false freedom of Tarshish stripped away, and underneath it stands a God who appoints the storm and the fish to bring you home. The running gets shaken off. The pursuing mercy does not.
reflection: Where am I running from something God has plainly asked of me?
What storm or swallowing has He used to halt my flight, and have I prayed yet?
Can I confess that salvation belongs to the LORD, and stop trying to outrun Him?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have run from You and called it freedom, and the running has cost me. Thank You that even now You pursue me, that the deep is Yours and so am I. In the dark of what my flight has cost, I confess it: salvation belongs to You. Bring me home. Amen.

notes.primary: Jonah 1:3 (Jonah flees from the presence of the LORD); Jonah 2:9 (salvation belongs to the LORD).

title: To whom shall we go?
moment: There is a break this phase has to name without flinching: people leave. Not a church, not a season, but Christ Himself. John records the hour bluntly. After a teaching too hard to swallow, many of Jesus' disciples drew back and walked with Him no more — not enemies, not outsiders, but followers, the crowd that had eaten the loaves and called Him good. Not every disconnect leads through a wilderness to a truer faith. Some lead away, full stop. Jesus does not chase them down the road or soften the saying to win them back. He turns instead to the Twelve, and the question He asks is terrible in its openness: do you also want to go away? He gives even His closest the room to leave. And into that silence Peter says the thing that holds, the answer that is not a boast but almost a groan: Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life. He does not stay because staying is easy or because his questions are answered. He stays because he has looked at the alternatives and found there is nowhere truer to walk.
voiceQuote: They went out from us, but they didn't belong to us; for if they had belonged to us, they would have continued with us.
scriptureText: Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life.
weight: In your own shaking you may feel the pull to walk away entirely — not merely from a congregation that wounded you, but from Christ. Before you go, sit with Peter's question, and let it be a real question and not a slogan. To whom would you actually go? The break that leaves Jesus behind leaves behind the words of eternal life, and nothing else on offer has them. There are honest reasons to doubt a church, to grieve a tradition, to walk out of a room that has become unbearable. Do those things if you must. But notice that none of them require leaving the only One who has the words of life. Peter stayed not because the teaching had gotten easy but because he had run the alternatives to their end and found them empty. That is the one reason to stay that survives the shaking — not that it is comfortable here, but that there is nowhere truer to go.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect must be honest that some breaks lead away from Christ, not toward Him. The phase will not coerce and it will not pretend the danger is unreal. What it asks of you is only this: before you walk away, answer Peter's question honestly — to whom would you go, if not to the One who has the words of eternal life?
upheaval.inYou: If you are tempted to leave Christ entirely, do not rush past Peter's question. To whom would you go? Doubt the church if you must; grieve what wounded you. But the break that leaves Jesus behind leaves the words of life behind too, and there is nowhere truer waiting. Do not lightly walk away from the only One who has them.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church watching people leave feels each departure as a wound, and some leavings prove final. John is honest about it: some go out because they were never truly of us. But the answer is neither panic nor pressure. It is to keep being the place that has, and freely offers, the words of eternal life, so that those who stay, stay for the only reason that holds.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the One the leavers leave. Crowds thin, followers turn back, the visible church loses its numbers in a season. But Christ still has the words of eternal life, and they do not become less true because some walk away from them. He remains, holding out life, when the room empties.
reflection: Am I being pulled to walk away not just from a church but from Christ Himself?
If I left, to whom would I actually go that has the words of eternal life?
What is the real reason I am staying, and is it one that will hold in the shaking?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, in this shaking I have felt the pull to leave You altogether. Before I take a step, let me hear Peter's question as my own: to whom would I go? You have the words of eternal life. Hold me when the teaching is hard. There is nowhere truer to go. Amen.

notes.primary: 1 John 2:19 (they went out from us); John 6:68 (Lord, to whom shall we go?).

title: A hundredfold
moment: A rich young man has just walked away, unable to make his break, his many possessions too heavy to set down. The disciples watch him go. And Peter, who has in fact left everything, says so out loud, half question and half ache: behold, we have left all and followed You. What about us? Jesus answers with the strangest arithmetic in the world. There is no one, He says, who has left house or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or land, for My sake and the gospel's, who will not receive a hundred times as much now in this present age — houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and land — and in the age to come, eternal life. He does not hide the cost; He folds it right into the promise, with persecutions, He says, in the same breath. But the shape of it is unmistakable. The break made for Christ is not subtraction. What looked like everything walking out the door comes back multiplied a hundredfold, in this life and not only the next. It is the math no ledger can hold: give it up for His sake, and it returns to you more than it ever was.
voiceQuote: There is no one who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or mother, or father, or children, or land, for my sake, and for the gospel's sake,
scriptureText: but he will receive one hundred times now in this time, houses, brothers, sisters, mothers, children, and land, with persecutions; and in the age to come, eternal life.
weight: Whatever you have genuinely left for Christ's sake — a relationship, a security, a standing, a whole former life — is not vanishing into a void. It can feel exactly like loss in the moment, because in the moment it is loss; the door really does close, and the room really does go quiet. But Jesus' promise reaches into the moment and past it. A hundredfold now, He says, with persecutions, and eternal life in the age to come. The break is real subtraction at the front edge and abundant addition at the final reckoning, and both are true at once. You are not throwing your life away by following Him into the rupture. You are investing it, at terms no earthly market offers — laying down what you had and receiving back, in this life and the next, more than you knew how to count. The cost is honest. So is the return.

upheaval.thePhase: Disconnect is loss, but never finally loss. The phase asks you to trust the arithmetic before you can see the return — to believe that what you set down for Christ's sake is not gone into nothing but planted, and that the breaking which costs you everything now is the front edge of a hundredfold you cannot yet count.
upheaval.inYou: Whatever you have truly left for Christ — people, security, a former life — is not lost into a void. Jesus promises a hundredfold return, persecutions and all, and eternal life beyond it. The break is real loss now and real gain in the end, both at once. You are not throwing your life away. You are investing it at terms the world cannot match.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church that asks people to leave much for the gospel must hold out Christ's own promise alongside the cost: the hundredfold, the new family of faith that receives the uprooted. The community is meant to be where the one who left house and kin finds a hundred homes and mothers and brothers. The body is how the promise becomes something a person can touch.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the promise underwriting the loss. The house you left can be taken, the family ties severed, the security stripped; the hundredfold and the eternal life Christ guaranteed cannot. When everything you surrendered for His sake is gone from sight, His word over it remains, and it returns what the shaking removed.
reflection: What have I genuinely left for Christ's sake, and have I grieved it as loss without seeing it as investment?
Do I believe the hundredfold is for now, with persecutions, and not only the age to come?
Where is God asking me to trust His arithmetic before I can see the return?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have counted what I left for You as pure loss, and forgotten Your promise over it. Teach me Your arithmetic: that what I surrender for Your sake is not gone but planted, returning a hundredfold now and eternal life beyond. Help me trust the gain I cannot yet see. Amen.

notes.primary: Mark 10:29-30 (no one who has left... will fail to receive a hundredfold, with persecutions, and eternal life).

title: Crucified with Christ
figure: Losing your life to find it
moment: Beneath every break in this whole movement lies one law, and Jesus states it without softening. Whoever desires to save his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for My sake will find it. There it is, the engine of the entire phase: the disconnect is, at the very bottom, a death — and that is precisely why it opens onto life. The instinct that feels like wisdom, the white-knuckled clutching of the old life to keep it safe, is the very thing that forfeits it. Paul says the same truth from the far side of having lived it, as starkly as language allows: I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I that live, but Christ living in me. Not improved, not reformed around the edges — crucified, the old self put to death so that a wholly other life could rise in its place. This reframes the whole break. The rupture is not the tragedy. The clutching is the tragedy. To die with Christ is not the catastrophe that befalls you in the upheaval; it is the doorway the upheaval is, all along, prying open.
voiceQuote: Whoever desires to save his life will lose it, and whoever will lose his life for my sake will find it.
scriptureText: I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I that live, but Christ living in me.
weight: The thing you are most afraid to lose in this break may be the very thing that, clutched, will cost you your life. That is the hard edge of Jesus' arithmetic, and it is also where the freedom hides. What you grasp to save, you forfeit; what you surrender to Him, you find — exactly, every time. So the question the upheaval keeps pressing is not how to hold on, but what you are still holding. The old self, the former security, the life you built and now defend with both hands — Jesus is not asking you to improve it. He is inviting you to let it die, and to discover that its death is not your ending. It is where Christ begins to live in you, where the I that strained and clutched gives way to a life that is no longer merely yours. The death is real. So is the resurrection on its other side. You are not being asked to lose for the sake of losing, but to lose for the sake of finding what clutching could never keep.

upheaval.thePhase: This is the deepest logic of Disconnect: the break is a death that turns out to be the only road to life. The phase asks you to stop reading the rupture as catastrophe and start reading it as crucifixion with Christ — the death of the old self that, far from ending you, is the very place He begins to live in you.
upheaval.inYou: The thing you are most afraid to lose may be the thing that, clutched, will cost you your life. Jesus' arithmetic is exact and freeing: what you grasp to save, you forfeit; what you surrender to Him, you find. The death of the old self is not your ending. It is where Christ begins to live in you, no longer merely you.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church trying to save its life — its buildings, its status, its survival — by clutching tends to lose the very thing it grasps for. The body willing to die with Christ, to lose its life for His sake, is the one that finds it. Institutional self-preservation is the slow death; crucifixion with Christ is the door to resurrection.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the life on the far side of the death. The old self can be crucified, the former existence lost, everything you clutched pried loose; the Christ who then lives in you cannot be removed. When the life you tried to save is gone, His life in you remains, and it is the only life death cannot take.
reflection: What am I most afraid to lose in this break, and am I clutching it in a way that will cost me my life?
Where am I trying to save the old self that Christ is inviting me to let die?
Can I believe that crucifixion with Christ is not my ending but where He begins to live in me?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have clutched the old life to save it, and feared the death this break is working in me. Teach me Your arithmetic: what I surrender to You, I find. Let the old self be crucified with You, and let it be true of me that Christ now lives in me. Amen.

notes.primary: Matthew 16:25 (lose your life to find it); Galatians 2:20 (crucified with Christ).

title: He goes before you
moment: The break ends one thing and pushes you out toward a country you never mapped. Israel stood exactly there. Moses, who had led them out and carried them this far, was dead and buried in Moab. Egypt and its old slavery were a generation gone, the wilderness behind them, and ahead lay only the Jordan and a strange land none of them had taken. It is the threshold every disconnect finally delivers you to: the old thing finished, the new thing not yet begun, and a river to cross into the unknown. And the word of the LORD to Joshua on that brink is not a battle plan. It is a presence. Be strong and courageous; do not be afraid, neither be dismayed, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go. Moses had already told them the heart of it: the LORD, He it is who goes before you; He will be with you, He will not fail you nor forsake you. The break does not end in abandonment on an empty shore. It ends with a God who has already crossed the river ahead of you, who walks into the trackless country first, and who will not leave you in it.
voiceQuote: Be strong and courageous; don't be afraid, neither be dismayed: for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go.
scriptureText: The LORD, he it is who goes before you; he will be with you, he will not fail you, neither forsake you.
weight: You have left. The old thing is behind you, finished, and there is no going back to it. And what lies ahead is unmapped and frightening, a far side of the river you cannot see across. This is where the break has been carrying you all along — not to a settled new home, not yet, but to the very edge of a wilderness. It would be easy to read the edge as the end, to stand on the bank and conclude that the breaking has simply deposited you nowhere. It has not. Hear Joshua's commission spoken over your own threshold: be strong and courageous, do not be dismayed, for the LORD your God goes with you into exactly the unknown you are dreading. He does not promise you the map. He promises you Himself, ahead of you and beside you, into the country you have never walked. The break was never abandonment. It was the long, hard road to a threshold where the God who goes before you is waiting to lead you across.

upheaval.thePhase: This is where Disconnect ends and Disorientation begins. The break has done its work: it has left the old behind and carried you to the river's edge, the trackless country just ahead. The phase asks one last thing as it hands you to the wilderness — to step in not alone but led, trusting that the LORD goes before you into the unknown.
upheaval.inYou: You have left; the old thing is behind you; and what lies ahead is unmapped and frightening. This is where the break delivers you — to the very edge of the wilderness. Hear Joshua's commission as your own: be strong, do not be dismayed, for the LORD your God goes with you into the unknown you are dreading, and will not forsake you there.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church on the far side of a break stands where Joshua stood — the old certainties gone, the new ground untaken and strange. The promise is the same one Israel received at the Jordan: God goes before His people into the unknown and will not forsake them in it. The body steps into the wilderness not alone but led, into the next long phase of the journey.
upheaval.whatRemains: What cannot be shaken is the One who goes before you. The old life is removed, the familiar ground left behind, the map taken away; the presence that crosses the river ahead of you remains. When everything that could be shaken is gone and only the unknown is left, He is in it already, and He will not fail you nor forsake you.
reflection: What threshold has my break delivered me to, and am I standing frozen on the bank?
Do I believe the LORD has already crossed into the unknown ahead of me?
Where do I need to hear, be strong and do not be dismayed, as a word spoken to me?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, the break has left me at the edge of a country I never mapped, and I am afraid to cross. Thank You that You go before me into it, that You will not fail me nor forsake me there. Make me strong and unafraid, and lead me into the unknown You have already entered. Amen.

notes.primary: Joshua 1:9 (be strong; the LORD is with you wherever you go); Deuteronomy 31:8 (he goes before you and will not forsake you).

title: Building the ark
era: The break with a whole world
moment: The order of the world has rotted past saving, and God resolves to begin again. The instructions to Noah are strange and exact: an ark of gopher wood, rooms inside it, the whole thing sealed within and without with pitch. So one man sets to work building a great box for a flood no one believes is coming, on dry ground, under a clear sky, while the neighbors watch and laugh. The labor goes on for years. There is no rain to vindicate him, no sign that the consensus is wrong and the lone builder right — only the word he was given, and the slow, public absurdity of obeying it. He cuts the timbers. He fits the rooms. He smears the pitch. Then the day comes that no one expected but the builder: come into the ark, the LORD says, for of all this generation He has found one man righteous before Him. The door shuts. The fountains of the deep break open, and the rain begins. The most total break in all of Scripture has come — God ending an entire corrupt world, and carrying one family and the seeds of life through the deluge in a wooden box.
voiceQuote: Make an ark of gopher wood; make rooms in the ark, and seal it inside and outside with pitch.
scriptureText: Come with all your household into the ark, for I have seen your righteousness before me in this generation.
weight: Sometimes faithfulness looks like building something the watching world finds absurd. You have heard, in the quiet, what is coming, and the building of your ark cuts you off from everyone who has not heard it — the friends who think you have lost your sense, the family who would rather you settled down and stopped your strange construction. Noah's break was not a single dramatic exit; it was years of obedient oddness before a single drop fell. That is the hard shape of this disconnect: the vindication comes late, if it comes in your sight at all, and in the meantime there is only the word you were given and the mockery you must build through. The ark you are asked to make may make sense to no one but God. So you measure the timbers anyway. You seal the seams anyway. The break that severs you from the doomed consensus around you is not madness; it is the one sane thing, even while everyone insists the sky is clear. The rain is the LORD's business. The building is yours.

upheaval.thePhase: This is Disconnect at its most total — God ending a whole corrupt order and carrying a remnant through the flood. The phase asks you to break with the consensus before the evidence arrives, on nothing but the word you were given, and to keep building through the mockery until the door at last is shut by a hand that is not yours.
upheaval.inYou: The ark you are building may make sense to no one but God, and the work may go on for years before anything justifies it. Your break is the long, public strangeness of obeying what only you have heard. Cut the timbers anyway. Faithfulness sometimes looks absurd to everyone but the One who asked for it.
upheaval.inTheBody: When an old order is past saving, God's way is often not to reform it but to carry a remnant through the judgment — an ark-people who broke with the doomed consensus in time. The church has been such an ark before, bearing the faith through the flood of a collapsing world while the world laughed at the building.
upheaval.whatRemains: The Builder of the ark, who shuts the door Himself. What cannot be shaken is that God never ends a world without preparing the vessel to carry life across it. When everything that can be flooded is swept away, the remnant He has sealed in remains, borne safely on the very waters that drown the rest.
reflection: What is God asking me to build that makes sense to no one around me?
Am I willing to obey before the evidence arrives, through years of looking foolish?
Where have I let the mockery of the watching world stop me from finishing the ark?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, You have asked me to build what no one else can see the need for, and the sky is still clear. Give me the nerve to keep cutting the timbers, to seal every seam, to obey before a single drop falls. The rain is Yours; the building is mine. Shut me safely in. Amen.

notes.primary: Genesis 6:14 (make an ark); Genesis 7:1 (come into the ark).

title: Sold into Egypt
moment: Joseph's break is not one he chose; it is done to him. His brothers, sick with envy, see him coming across the field and decide to be rid of him. They strip off the coat their father gave him and throw him into a dry pit, and then, when a caravan of traders happens by, they haul him up and sell him for twenty pieces of silver. He is dragged off to Egypt, a teenage boy torn from his father and his home by the very people who should have kept him safe. This is the break of betrayal — not a wilderness God called him into, but a wound others inflicted on him. Years pass. He is enslaved, falsely accused, forgotten in a prison. And then, by a road no one could have plotted, he stands as the second man in Egypt, holding over his trembling brothers the power to destroy them. He weeps instead. He says the words that have echoed ever since: what they meant against him for evil, God had meant for good, to keep many people alive. The break others inflicted, God had been quietly weaving, all along, into rescue.
voiceQuote: Midianite merchants passed by, and they drew Joseph up out of the pit, and sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver; and they brought Joseph into Egypt.
voiceAttribution: Of Joseph, sold by his brothers — Genesis 37:28 (WEB)
scriptureText: As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to save many people alive.
weight: Some of your breaks were not chosen. They were inflicted — a betrayal, a casting-out, a wound delivered by the people who were supposed to protect you. There is a particular bitterness to that kind of disconnect: you did nothing to invite it, and it came anyway, from the hands you trusted most. Notice that Joseph never pretends it was something other than what it was. He does not say they meant well, or that it did not really hurt. He looks his brothers in the face and names it: you meant evil against me. The evil was real. And yet, on the far side of long years, he can also say the other thing — but God meant it for good. Both are true at once. The break done against you is genuinely evil, and it is not beyond the reach of a God who works even betrayal toward life. You do not have to whitewash the wound to trust the weaving. Hold the evil and the good in the same breath, as Joseph did, and let the second word outlast the first.

upheaval.thePhase: This is Disconnect inflicted, not chosen — the break others lay on you through betrayal. The phase does not ask you to call the evil good or to pretend the wound away. It asks you to trust that the God who is in the shaking can take even what was meant against you and weave it, in time, toward the saving of many lives.
upheaval.inYou: Some of your breaks were done to you — a betrayal, a casting-out, a wound from people who should have kept you safe. Joseph never pretends it was not evil. But in time he could say God meant it for good. The break inflicted against you is not beyond the reach of a God who works even betrayal toward life.
upheaval.inTheBody: The church has been broken by betrayal from within, and God has a long record of weaving even those wounds into a wider rescue. This is no excuse for the betrayal, and it never softens it. But it is a reason not to despair of it. What was meant for evil against the body, God is able to mean for good.
upheaval.whatRemains: The hand that weaves the betrayal toward good. What cannot be shaken is the providence beneath the wound — a God who is not absent from the pit or the sale or the prison, but quietly turning even the worst thing done to you toward life. The evil is real and passing; the weaving outlasts it.
reflection: What break in my life was inflicted on me rather than chosen?
Can I name the evil honestly and still trust that God is weaving it toward good?
Where am I being asked to release a betrayal into the hands of the One who redeems it?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, this break was done to me, and it was wrong; I will not pretend otherwise. Yet I have seen that You are not absent from the pit. Weave even this betrayal toward life, as You have done before. Let Your good, in time, be the word that outlasts the evil. Amen.

notes.primary: Genesis 37:28 (Joseph sold into Egypt); Genesis 50:20 (you meant evil, God meant good).

title: Forty years by the well
moment: Moses' first attempt at deliverance ends in a corpse and a panic. He sees an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, looks both ways, kills the man, and buries him in the sand — and the next day learns the thing is known. So the prince of Egypt becomes a fugitive overnight, fleeing for his life from the face of Pharaoh, and the chapter that should have launched his calling instead collapses it. He ends up far away in the land of Midian, and there, drained and undone, he simply sits down by a well. And there he stays. Forty years he stays — tending another man's sheep on the back side of the desert, the prince turned shepherd, the deliverer turned nobody, apparently forgotten by everyone, including, it must have seemed, God. No voice, no sign, no rescue. Only the long silence of obscurity, decade after decade, the old dream of saving his people buried as deep as the Egyptian in the sand. And then, when forty years are fulfilled, an angel of the Lord appears to him out in that wilderness, in a bush wrapped in flame and not consumed. Only after the silent decades does the bush at last begin to burn.
voiceQuote: Moses fled from the face of Pharaoh, and lived in the land of Midian; and he sat down by a well.
scriptureText: When forty years were fulfilled, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush.
weight: Some breaks drop you into a long obscurity. Not a dramatic loss with a clear end, but a wilderness season where nothing visibly happens, where the old dream looks dead and buried and you are tending sheep on the back side of nowhere, sure you have been forgotten. The hardest part is the length of it. A short trial you can endure on adrenaline; it is the decades that test you — the years with no voice, no sign, no evidence the silence will ever break. Moses sat by that well for forty years. From the inside it must have looked exactly like a story quietly ending. It was not. It was the hidden preparation for the thing he could never have done as the impatient prince who killed a man and ran. The break that feels like your life going nowhere may be the long obscurity in which God is forming you out of sight. The shepherd's years were not the deliverer's waste; they were his making. Do not despise the well, or the silence, or the sheep. The bush burns in its own time.

upheaval.thePhase: This is the long Disconnect of exile and obscurity — the break that drops you into hidden, fallow years before the call. The phase asks for endurance more than nerve: to stay faithful through decades when nothing visibly happens, to let yourself be quietly formed in a place no one is watching, and to trust that the silence is preparation, not abandonment.
upheaval.inYou: Some breaks drop you into a long obscurity — a wilderness season where nothing visibly happens and the old dream looks dead. Moses spent forty years there before the bush. The break that feels like your story quietly ending may be the hidden decades in which God is preparing you for what you could never have done before.
upheaval.inTheBody: Renewers are often formed in obscurity, broken off from prominence for long seasons before God calls them out. A church should not despise its hidden, fallow years. The wilderness of obscurity is where God has prepared more than one deliverer the people had long since given up on, and forgotten by the well.
upheaval.whatRemains: The God who has not forgotten the man by the well. What cannot be shaken is that the silence is not absence; the long obscurity is His workshop, not His neglect. When the visible story seems to have ended and every dream lies buried, the One forming you in the dark remains, and in His time the bush still burns.
reflection: Where am I sitting by a well, sure I have been forgotten?
Can I trust that the silent, obscure season is preparing me rather than wasting me?
What is God forming in me, out of sight, that the impatient old version of me could never have carried?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have been a long time by this well, and the silence makes me feel forgotten. Teach me that obscurity is Your workshop, not Your neglect. Form in me, out of sight, what I could never have become in the spotlight. And when the time is full, let the bush burn. Amen.

notes.primary: Exodus 2:15 (Moses flees to Midian); Acts 7:30 (forty years later, the burning bush).

title: Tear down the altar
moment: Before Gideon can ever face the enemy outside, God hands him a smaller, harder assignment first. The Midianites are crushing Israel, and Gideon wants to fight them — but the LORD points him, that very night, in another direction entirely: take your father's bull, and pull down the altar of Baal that stands in your father's own household, and cut down the Asherah beside it. Not the enemy army. His own father's altar. The first break God asks of the deliverer is against the idolatry standing in his own family's yard, the false gods his own household has kept and served. It is a frightening order, because it will cost him not on a distant battlefield but at home, where the offense will land hardest and the reprisal could be swift. And Gideon does it. He is afraid — the text says so plainly, that dread of his own household and of the townsmen drove him to act under cover of dark. So he takes ten servants and goes out by night and pulls the altar down. Trembling, in the dark, hiding his face — but down it comes. The disconnect from inherited idolatry begins, as it so often does, first and at home and in fear.
voiceQuote: Take your father's bull... and throw down the altar of Baal that your father has, and cut down the Asherah that is by it.
scriptureText: Gideon took ten of his servants, and did as the LORD had spoken to him; and because he feared his father's household and the men of the city, he did it by night.
weight: The hardest idols to break with are almost never the obvious, distant ones. They are the ones you inherited — the family gods, the assumptions you absorbed growing up, the altars no one in your household ever questioned because they had simply always stood there. Breaking with those costs you where it hurts most: at home, among the people whose approval you most want, who will take the demolition as a personal insult. So notice what Gideon's night raid quietly teaches. He was afraid. He did not feel brave; he felt the fear so sharply that he waited for darkness and hid his face. And he tore the altar down anyway. That is the thing to hold onto. Courage is not the absence of fear, and a break does not have to be fearless to be true obedience.
